House again in committee to consider a certain proposed' resolution to amend the Civil Service Act (p. 11829).
On section 10,
I would like to ask the hon. Postmaster Genex-al (Hon. Sir William Muiock) if provision is made for statutory increases for third-class clerks ?
Yes ; section 13 meets the case.
What does that say ?

(reading) :
The Governor in Council may, after a third class clerk has served one year, increase his salary, by the amourcs not exceeding $51 in anyone year, up to the maximum salary of a third class clerk hereinbefore provided for.
Section 10 provides for the creation of a new class. At the present time there is throughout the service a large number of temporary clerks and temporary writers. In 1895 the old third-class clerkship was abolished, and since then all new appointments below the rank of second-class, or since we created the rank of junior second-class, below the rank of junior second-class have been temporary writers. If this section is adopted there will then be a class to which temporary writers and temporary clerks may eventually be transferred.
What is the advantage of creating more third-class clerks ? Why should you have a lower order of clerks ? I do not see the advantage of it.
Surely $500 a year is a low enough minimum salary ?
I do not object to the salary.
What does tlie hon. gentleman object to ?
Why should you increase the number of third-class clerks instead of making a higher grade ?
There Is no third-class clerkship now.
If it were abolished, it must have been abolished for some reason. Whether it was a good one or a bad one, what are the reasons for reviving it ?

I am not justifying the abolition of the third-class clerkship, when it was abolished in 1895. Sufficient to say that it was abolished. The present government, having had some years' experience iu the working of the system without there being a class of permanent officers 'below the junior second, has come to the conclusion that it is in the public interest that a third-class shall be established. At the present time there is throughout the inside service a considerable number of persons holding the rank of temporaries. These persons are temporary clerks and temporary writers. The statute of 1895, which abolished third-class clerkships, contained a provision for temporary appointments. Under that provision a temporary appointed as a clerk or a writer commences at $400 and became eligible for an annual increase of $30 a year until the maximum of $000 was attained. Any one will see that remuneration of that kind to-day for even a clerical position in any one of the departments is wholly inadequate to enable the clerk to live properly or to; maintain even a reasonable appearance. ' It is not said that everybody who is in a temporary class ought to be transferred to this permanent class, but I trust that the government will make a liberal _use of this provision, and transfer from the temporary class of writers and clerks those who are deserving of promotion to the permanent list. If any of them at the time of the transfer are in receipt of less than $500 they will at once become entitled to $500, the minimum of the third-class. If th'ey are in receipt of more than $500 they will carry that salary into the permanent class, and once they are in the permanent class they will be eligible, not for an increase of $30 a year, but for an increase of $50 a year until they obtain the maximum, not of $000, but of $700, which is the maximum of a third-class clerk.

The lion. Postmaster General, either intentionally or innocently, entirely misunderstood the point of my question. I do not need to be told that it is necessary to increase the salaries of the civil service, and particularly of those clerks who are receiving smaller salaries and holding the inferior positions. I asked the hon. Postmaster General why he was creating this third-class order of clerks instead of increasing the second-class. It seems to me that the fact that this third-class grade was abolished in 1895 shows that there must have been some reason for the abolition. The idea. I fancy, was to get a superior class of men. If yon have the ordinary third-class clerks, you will naturally get a more inferior class of men than you would if you had more junior second-class clerks. A high qualification should be exacted from men seeking positions in the civil service. This is what a business man would do. It seems to me that you are not accomplishing much by instituting the order of third-class
clerks. If you have not that class, the temporary clerks who are fit for duty could then be promoted to the higher class.

I would like to ask the hon. Postmaster General if this measure deals exclusively with the inside service, leaving untouched the anomaly that now exists in the outside service, where many men, in the public works and other departments, who have been a long time in the service, cannot get promotion, no matter how valuable their services may he, because they are only on the temporary list ?

This measure does not deal with every branch of the service, inside and outside. We are dealing with the civil service from time to time, endeavouring to consider and deal with all cases. Rut no government has ever yet reorganized the whole civil service of Canada at one stroke. We are doing it by instalments, as this measure and previous measures indicate. For example, the department of the public service that, compared with other departments, represents by far the greatest number of civil servants is the Post Office Department, which contains about one-third of the whole service. Last year and this year there has been legislation _ dealing with both the outside and the inside ' service of the Post Office Department, improving the position of many classes of employees. I do not remember whether prior to the present session there has been legislation by this government with reference to the outside service of other departments. At all events, if my hon. friend will refer to section 15 of the resolution, he will observe that it deals with the outside service of the Customs and Inland Revenue Departments, which represent a considerable number of officers.

There are some very aggravated cases of injustice in the outside service which ought to be dealt with. This is not a new matter: it has been in existence for many years. The hon. Postmaster General will perhaps remember that many cases have been mentioned during the discussion of the estimates in connection with the Department of Public Works where men have been kept on from year to year without any opportunities of promotion on the ground of merit. It seems to me that while one branch of the service is being dealt with, the hon. Postmaster General might well go further and deal with the cases to which I refer.

I do not think the great majority of the officers of the Public Works Department, who are technical officers, would take employment from the department at salaries provided in this Bill for the permanent staff. They receive two or three times the pay of the ordinary departmental clerk, and no doubt are worthy of it. I think the great majority of the employees in the outside service are
1250!

pretty well satisfied with the pay they receive. In these eases the department has to meet public competition. These men cam get employment anywhere; they are not hanging on to the service for employment, as some of the permanent service are. I am inclined to think that they are generally treated on their merits. When application is made for increased payment, it is considered. We are not limited by the Civil Service Act in these cases, and I am not aware that there is any particular complaint on the part of the outside officials of the Public Works Department in regard to the pay they are receiving.

I cannot agree with the lion. Minister of Public Works as to the true principle. He seems to be of the opinion that the proper thing is to have the increase of pay dependent on the will of the head of the department. Now, it seems to me a very important thing, in connection with civil service salary reform, that the principle should be adopted and established of a statutory increase of salary from the minimum to. the maximum, and that that increase should not be dependent on the whim or the will of the chief or the deputy chief of the department. As I pointed out the other night, that leads to favouritism and to toadyism, two things which are very detrimental to the proper working of any department. I had hoped that the Postmaster General would have taken that matter into consideration.

I cannot agree with the hon. member at all. Theoretically there might be something in what he says; but what does it practically mean ? It means that the deputy ministers in the public service of Canada are incapable, incompetent, dishonest, full of partisanship.
No, no.

That is what it involves. In banking, financial and commercial institutions the men at the head are supposed to he capable of reporting to their board what men are competent and faithful and should be paid accordingly. It is possible that a deputy minister may in some eases be influenced by feelings of friendship or similar reasons; but I cannot imagine that a man occupying the position of deputy minister in the public service would be so incompetent and so weak as to prevent a good official receiving the pay he is entitled to, or to increase the salary of another simply because he toadies to him.
A horrible thing, that.

I cannot think that men holding such important positions would be influenced by such improper motives. I cannot say that I have found political influence or favouritism have had weight with the deputy minister. In almost every department the deputy Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
is an opponent of the present government or at least w'hose political sympathies were with the present opposition, but is not my experience that they have been influenced in their recommendations by the unworthy motives suggested by the hon. member for King's (Mr. Fowler). What appears to be the curse of the civil service is that every employee gets paid according to an Act of parliament, no matter what may be his habits or abilities. He is there permanently, and goes on drawing his salary whether he attends to his duties or not or is capable of doing them or not. If the deputy minister had more control over those under him, had more to say about the way they did their work, perhaps the work would be better done. But I do not believe that the deputy ministers are influenced by any such improper motives as the hon. member for King's thinks they are.

The head of the department stands in a very different position from the head of a banking institution. The latter finds it necessary to employ the very best men he can get in order that the bank may make money for its shareholders. He cannot allow himself to be influenced by favoritism, but must have a keen eye to the interests of the bank. The case is altogether different in a government department. It is not a money-making department, and therefore is more susceptible to favouritism. I have no desire to limit the powers of the two ministers. I think it is absolutely essential for the well-working of the department that the deputy head should have a great deal of control over the clerks ; and if there are any who will not do their work properly, they should be dismissed. I have not made any charge against the heads of departments, but the hon. minister has made a very serious charge against the employees generally, because he has said that if these increases were statutory the clerks would not do their duty. I do not believe that follows as a natural consequence. The only fair way is to make these increases statutory. I believe in paying a man well for doing good work, and I think that we ought to have in the civil service the best class of men we can get. In order to do that, we have to compete with public institutions which give their men first-class pay. As business men, we want to have the most practical system, and the only practical method is to make these increases statutory, and thus do away with the favouritism and toadyism which to-day prevail. The hon. minister may say what he likes, but he himself is governed by his political feelings, and is touched with the same infirmities as other human beings.
What are they V

My hon. friend has experienced most of the infirmities that afflict

human nature, and therefore the question is a very unnecessary one for him to ask.

In the case of bank clerks, their salaries are increased from time to time according to merit. I have had some experience with public departments here, and I have come to the conclusion that as a rule they are manned by capable men, whom it would be hard to replace. Their knowledge of the work entitles them to a great deal of consideration, and I do not think it would be well to have their salaries statutory, but they should be increased according to merit and time of service.

Some reference has been made by myself andi others to the technical officers in the departments of the Interior, Railways and Canals and Public Works. I do not know that anything has been said about a certain number of officers who are temporary clerks and whose cases deserve considerable consideration. I refer to gentlemen performing the duties of clerks, assistant accountants, and so on, of whom, I believe, there is a number, more particularly in the Department of Public Works. Some of these have been employed for a number of years.
Why are they not permanent ?

I do not know. Some of them have been as long in the department as fifteen years. It seems to me an anomaly that gentlemen should be that long in the service and be still only on the temporary list. That leads to log-rolling and political pull and affects the independence of the civil service. I know that at this juncture, when the session is about to close, and any delay would imperil the passing of this Bill, it would not be advisable to make any amendment. But I take this opportunity of calling the attention of the Minister of Public Works to the fact.

I have endeavoured to get information on the very matter which the hon. gentleman has just mentioned. Earlier in the session the Minister of Customs introduced a measure affecting some' of the civil servants, and I then endeavoured to ascertain why men, who had been from ten to fifteen years in the public service, should still be regarded as temporary clerks. There is no doubt that the intention is that the duties performed by these men shall be performed every year by some officer, yet in certain departments of the government service we have a large number of men holding the status of temporary employees who have been in these positions for ten, twelve or fifteen years. There may be some good reason for this, but on former occasions the hon. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) has not been able to convince me that there is any good reason, and on the present occasion no good reason has
been advanced. It is true that it is late in the session, but, if the government is not able to fully consider a matter of this kind and to bring down a measure dealing with it iu a comprehensive manner in a six months' session, I do not know when we can expect to have it dealt with or to have the anomaly to which my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) has called attention, ended. Perhaps in the absence of the Postmaster General the Minister of Public Works could explain why this anomaly still continues to exist not only in his department, but also in the Departments of Customs and, I believe, of Railways and Canals.

I fear I will have to admit that I am unable to explain why this condition exists in my department. During the short time I have been in the department the House has been in session and other important matters iu connection with the department and with other public business have pressed upon my attention. Therefore I have been able to give the question of the service very little attention. Representations have been made to me in regard to this matter and I have discussed it with the deputy minister. While there may be something in the statement made as to possible favouritism by a ideputy minister. I am satisfied that no department can be properly controlled unless the head of the department has considerable influence over the employees under him. I am in favour of removing the service as much as possible from any political influence. A political minister as my hon. friend says even without any great infirmities or weakness of human nature might be inclined to favour his friends at the expense of others. I am of the opinion that the kindest service this House could render to the permanent civil service would be to have them disfranchised ; that. I feel, would have a splendid effect in putting an end to the exercise of political influence by members of the service to procure their own advancement. So far as the temporary employees in the Public Works Department are concerned, I may say that the department is at the present time carrying on very considerable works which require the employment of foremen, engineers, draughtsmen, and other employees of that description whose services may be dispensed with at the end of three or six months or at the completion of some of these works. It would be impossible to have ai permanent list of all these employees ns the amount of work varies so much from time 1o time. This accounts for a good many of these temporary employees. As to those employed in the office in Ottawa, I imagine, from the little conversation I have had with the deputy minister, that the condition is accounted for by the great increase in. the business of the department. If one will look at the growth of the department he will see that in a few years there lias been a change from an expenditure of some-

thing less than a million dollars to an expenditure of eight or ten million dollars a year and consequently the work has grown immensely.
Mr. CLAItKE. That is a startling increase.

A startling increase owing solely to the great progress that is being made by the country. As I say the work of the department inis increased very largely and very rapidly and it may be that employees taken on in connection with a particular work have been continued in these positions owing to other work of the same kind being undertaken. I am not in a position, in reply to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) to offer an opinion as to whether it would be in the interest of the public or of the civil service that the permanent list should be increased. Since attention has been called to this matter I shall ask the Deputy Minister of Public Works for a report as to whether in his opinion it would be in the interest of the public that the permanent list should be increased and how he accounts for what the hon. leader of the opposition has called this large temporary list that seems to be almost continuous.

In reference to the Customs Department I may say that the explanations I gave at the time this question was up before were, as usual, very clear, and I have no doubt that my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) at that time understood them although the explanation has escaped his piemory in the meantime. I do not think there is much trouble of this kind in connection with the inside service of the Customs Department. We have some officers paid out of contingencies, but as to their going on the permanent staff I may say that the deputy minister deals with that matter and that his recommendations have usually met with my approval. There are a great many men in the outside service who have been on for a long time who are not on. the permanent staff, but who are very anxious to get on it. The way in which they would get on the temporary list would be as acting landing waiters or other positions, and they are anxious to be put on as preventive officers, the one loop-hole in the Civil Service Act through which they can get on the permanent list without passing the civil service examination. We have on the permanent list, under the general class of preventive officers, a large number of men and their salaries may run from $400 to $4,000. The Civil Service Act is silent on that point. And we have put on some of the older hands who have worked for a great many years and who could not pass this what might be called literary examination, an examination which in my opinion is not very valuable in the case of those officers. In the very Bill which is being introduced by the hon. the Postmaster Gene-Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
ral (Sir William Mulock) there is a provision for the substitution of a practical examination for this literary examination called for by the Civil Service Act iu cases where the commissioner of customs deems it advisable to employ the practical examination so that these parties on successfully undergoing their practical examination will be able to go on the permanent list.
In the old days when they contributed to the superannuation fund it was a matter of more importance to be on the permanent list, so that when the time arrived that he wished to take superannuation, then be had an allowance. Now, when they retire from the permanent list they get simply their own money which has been retained from them year after year, with compound interest under the new law. There is therefore not as great a desire to get on the permanent list as there was before. But a permanent employee is entitled, if possible, to his three weeks holidays. If he should be absent for sickness during a day or week, his salary his paid. While lie remains on the temporary list, though he has been an officer of the government for fifteen or twenty years, if he loses any time by sickness. it is deducted. With reference to the outside service- in the customs, I have thought over the matter a great deal since the subject was discussed by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) and others, though it had been in my mind before ; and the Postmaster General agrees with me that in the Bill which will be founded on this resolution, we will be able in a case of this kind to substitute a practical examination instead of a literary examination, and thus put them on the permanent list. Though they could not pass the test of the ordinary civil service examination prescribed by the law, yet we will have the satisfaction of knowing that we are putting upon the permanent list men who are fully capable of discharging the particular duties to which they have been assigned.

My hon. friend has paid a great compliment to his powers of luminous exposition, and it may be that I understood the matter as well as he thinks I did at the time. I cannot say, however, that he has made it remarkably clear. The difficulty I had is this, why men who are, as pointed out by my hon. friend from Ottawa, kept on continuously ten, twelve or fifteen years, should be retained as mere temporary employees when we know that their services will be required in the future just as much as they have been in the past ten years, or for even a greater period. Sly hon. friend explains that as far ns the Department of Customs is concerned it apparently turns altogether on their inability to pass the examinations in that connection.

It is the spirit of the Civil Service Act, that they

should pass tlie examination prescribed by tlie civil service examiners, and that is largely a test that, when a young man comes out of school, he perhaps could answer ; but after a lapse of years there are many in the civil service who will not attempt it, because they feel they could not do it, though they are fully able to perform the duties assigned to them. That has been the trouble so far as the customs is concerned.
Have there not been some of these men perfectly willing to undertake that examination ?

Yes, but in every case where they write to me and ask to get on the permanent list, I say : AVe should be only too glad to recommend you to council for permanent employment if you pass the examination. I think invariably I make that reply, and a great many have done it, mostly the younger men that have entered the service lately. But with reference to the older ones that have been in the departments ten or twelve years, they say : AVell. we do not think we should be asked to do it.

If a man has been discharging certain duties as a temporary employee for ten or twelve years it would seem to me to be father an anomaly that, because he cannot pass a particular examination, he Should be excluded from performing those same duties any longer as a permanent employee. My boil, friend sees the anomaly, yet it has been allowed to exist for many years. The anomaly has no doubt increased during the past six or seven years on account of the necessity of employing more of these temporary men. *
I propose to remedy that now, if the House will consent to the alterations in the Bill substituting a practical examination.

I should think it would be a desirable thing to do, because if men have been discharging these duties for a number of years as temporary employees, there cannot be any great reason for keeping them in that class of temporary employees simply because they cannot pass some examination which lias not been found necessary for the discharge of their duties in the past. I would like to ask my hon. friend the Postmaster General just what is the effect of this amendment provided for in clause 10 of the resolution. I do not regard this as a very wise way of amending a statute, because it always leaves us in doubt as to what is accomplished. I should think the better course woidd be to give us the section as proposed to be amended.
There is no amendment to section 10.

I am speaking of clause 10 of the resolution, which introduces an amendment to schedule A of the Civil Service Act. AVkat is exactly the meaning of the expression 1 third-class clerks ' in schedule A ?

The effect is to create an additional class. This amendment to schedule A of the Civil Service Act merely adds an additional class which will be available for persons that may hereafter be appointed to the service, or who may now be temporarily in the service. My hon. friend will see by reference to sections 33 and 34 that persons may be transferred to the third class. It is not intended to transfer every one that is now a temporary clerk or writer to the third class, although I think that a liberal use will be made of this jjrovision. Still there may be some persons in the ranks of temporary clerks and writers who may not be transferred, but this will make it possible to promote them to that class. All temporary clerks and writers must have passed the qualifying examination.
AVill anybody be eligible to promotion to this third class as temporary writers or clerks who have not passed the civil service examination ?

They could not be temporary clerks or writers without having passed the qualifying examination. Under this provision I have no doubt any one could get into the third class without passing the civil service examination. There is nothing in this Bill affecting generally the question of examination of persons who are temporary clerks and temporary writers. Under the old law they were obliged to pass an examination.
Has that law been enforced V
Of course, we could not disregard the statute. It would be impossible to waive the statute requiring a fulfilment of the conditions prescribed by the law.

It must be patent to every member of this House how difficult it is to bring in a Bill hurriedly and give proper consideration to all the members of the service. It seems to me that the road that the hon. Postmaster General has got upon is the right way and that the second set of resolutions which he has introduced will meet with the approval of the service as far as they go. I am sorry, however, that the hon. Postmaster General will not meet the views of members of the opposition and go the additional length that I suggested in my amendment. But let this Bill pass now and with the view of dealing more justly, fairly and uniformly with all tlie departments, if the hon. Postmaster General will allow me. I will make the following suggestion :	That the members
of the government appoint a committee to

deal with this question in a business sort of way, to ascertain from the various heads of the departments the different classes of clerks, permanent, technical and otherwise employed in the various departments with the salaries now received and the work now performed with the object of making a complete and uniform revision of civil service salaries and that the said committee report this session, or during the session of 1904. It would probably be asking too much to ask them to report this session. I think if the government would do something of that sort it would do away with this picayune way of dealing with such an important subject as the Civil Service Act. I think we should deal with it in a more business'ike way than that in which we are now dealing with it. By dealing with one class and not with another we offend the class whose claims are not considered. I am satisfied that what the government want to do, and it is what I desire to do myself, is to deal with all classes of the service equally and to deal with each according to its merits.
I am very much surprised that my boil. friend (Mr. Birkett) makes such a motion as that at this stage.
I am not making a motion. I am merely offering a suggestion.

Well, a suggestion. 1 beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. My hon. friend should not fly off in that way. I did not intend to say anything offensive. I am very much surprised that my hon. friend should make such a suggestion at this stage

Why ?
Mr. BEIjOOTJRT. Because it means the withdrawal of this Bill.
I do not object to the Bill.
The adoption of this suggestion means that this Bill shall be withdrawn.
Not at all.
It cannot mean anything else.
Did you read the suggestion V

It is that :
The government appoint a committee to ascertain from the various heads ot the departments the different classes of clerks, permanent, technical and otherwise employed in the various departments with the salaries now received and the work now performed with the object of making a complete and uniform revision of the civil service salaries and that said committee report at this session.
During the present session it would be impossible to have an investigation made and the report of the committee submitted to this House in order that we could deal with it and the only result of the suggestion Mr. BIRKETT.
if acted upon would be that the government would have to withdraw the Bill and this very substantial measure of relief which it proposes to give to the civil service would not be given.
Not at ail.
I think so.

Surely the hon. gentleman (Mr. Belcourt) must have been paying no attention to the remarks of my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Birkett). He accepted the Bill of the hon. Postmaster General as an instalment of justice to the civil service but he suggested in a most respectful and courteous manner, that justice may be done to all classes of the civil service, that a committee such as he suggested might be appointed and that if it could not make a report at this session it might bring its report before parliament at a subsequent session. I thought it was a most admirable and valuable suggestion and I thought it was made to the hon. Postmaster General in the kindliest possible spirit in order to do full justice to all classes of the civil service. I myself am of the opinion that there are in the civil service a great many persons who are underpaid and that there are a great many who are deserving of consideration, and in case that class should go without reasonable consideration my horn, friend makes the very reasonable suggestion, that, to enable the hon. Postmaster General to deal out that even handed justice to the civil service to which it is entitled, a commission be appointed to inquire into the whole matter. My hon. friend has submitted that suggestion because of the deep interest he takes in the welfare of the civil service and because he is trying to do justice to the civil service without favour or affection.

I would be only too pleased to accept all practical suggestions which have for their object the rendering of justice to all branches of the civil service. But, when I consider this proposition the question is how acquiescence might meet the present exigency. The hon. gentleman stated that under the present Bill it is proposed to deal with the civil service in a picayune manner. If the Bill only deals with the service in a picayune manner and if he is not favourable to picayune legislation be therefore disapproves of this measure. He cannot approbate and reprobate at the same moment. What does be propose ? It is quite clear that this suggestion does not only apply to those who are not dealt with by this Bill, but that it also applies to those whom it is proposed to deal with by this Bill. It would seem to be rather inexpedient for ns to undertake the task of considering the salaries and duties of all those whose case may be dealt with in this measure. The proper time to deal with matters of that kind is, I presume, before promotions are made. The government have enough 'information to go a certain distance and to go such a dist-

ance as this measure proposes. The non. gentleman's suggestion is :
That the government appoint a committee to ascertain from the various heads of the departments the different classes of clerks, permanent, technical and otherwise-
The word ' otherwise ' means the outside service, perhaps; I will not say. It is not mentioned. But ' otherwise,' must embrace temporary clerks and writers all of whom are subject to the legislation which we are now proposing. The suggestion is that:
The government appoint a committee (to ascertain from the various heads of the departments the different classes of clerks, permanent, technical and otherwise employed in the various departments, with the salaries now received and the work now performed with the object of making a complete and uniform revision of civil service salaries and that said committee report this session with as little delay as possible.
There are in the civil service a great many hundreds of clerks of various kinds, temporary, technical and permanent, such as are mentioned in this suggestion. How long would it take the committee to perform this work ? I do not know how you are going to constitute the committee. Does the hon. gentleman propose that it should be a committee of this House ?
Mr. BIRKETT- No, I suggest the deputy heads of the departments.

That is not the hon. gentleman's suggestion. The hon. gentleman's suggestion is that there should be a committee appointed to ascertain from tbe heads of the departments. Therefore tbe committee he proposes is not a committee of the deputy heads. This is the language :
That the government appoint a committee to ascertain from the heads.
This is a committee to consult with the deputy heads.
A committee of the Privy Council.
I do not know what committee is proposed.

I did not name the committee. This is merely a suggestion I made to the government asking that they appoint a committee. It would then be at the discretion of the government to appoint whatever committee they thought fit-a committee composed of the deputy heads, chief clerks or any other persons.
That is the government is to appoint a committee to interview the deputy heads and to have the deputy heads report.
That is not my suggestion.

This is the suggestion :	That the government appoint a committee to ascertain from the various heads of departments. The heads of the departments are the ministers ; so it is not the deputy heads who are to be consulted. The committee is to consult with the ministers to obtain the names of the various classes of civil servants, their work and their proper emolument, and to report this session. I suppose this session will come to an end some time.

If the hon. Postmaster General will allow me a moment, he will see, if he refers to the memorandum, that I struck out that portion, which is blurred, and said either the- session of 1903 or the session of 1904. The hon. gentleman is trying to make the most of that; but I hope he will be bonest and take the suggestion in the same spirit in which I make ft.

I thought the hon. gentleman was desirous that the report should be made this session, and therefore I assumed that the last few words were intended to be part of the suggestion. In justice to him, I thought it would be altogether more iu accordance with his interests and views if he could show that he had proposed the appointment of a committee to report this session. However, since he does not desire that, since he would strike out the last words, ' this session, with as little delay as possible,' then it would seem that he is quite willing that the whole matter should be referred to a committee to make a report as soon as possible, this session or next session. Now, I doubt if it would be in accordance with the views of a considerable number of the civil servants who will he affected by this measure, if we were to accept any proposition looking to delay. The hon. gentleman, I have no doubt, would repudiate any desire to occasion delay.
He has already done so.

The hon. member for Ottawa is well able to defend himself. He rarely honours us with his suggestions, and he may be allowed to speak for himself, although no doubt the father of the House from West Toronto will take him under his wing at the proper time, as he does on many occasions. But at the present moment we are dealing with a proposition to advance a large number of the civil servants. I was asked by a member of the opposition why we were reviving the third-class clerkship when there must have been a good reason for abolishing that class in 1895. I have before me ' Hansard ' of 1895, which throws some light on the reasons for the abolition of that class. It appears that the Bill was introduced by the Hon. Dr. Montague, who, in moving the first reading, spoke as follows :
The main (provision of the Bill does ajvay with the class of civil servants known as third-class clerks. In order to perform the work done by that class, the government by this Bill



take power to employ writers, who will begin at $400 ia year and reach alter a time a maximum of $600 a year. Of course, the Bill will not affect in any way the third-class clerks now in the service ; it only applies to future appointments.
These were the only remarks made by any person on the introduction of the Bill. When it came up for its second reading, Dr. Montague gave the reasons for the introduction of the Bill. He said :
I think (there is one point on which we can all agree ; that is, that when the civil service was constituted, the permanency which was then given to the service was for the purpose of securing for the performance of the more important duties the very best class of men who could be secured. It w,as to be an encouragement for men of high qualifications to apply for and accept positions in the service ; and the same idea, I fancy, ran through the minds of this parliament when it constituted a superannuation system. There is no doubt that, as regards the higher offices in the service, the feature lof permanency has worked very well indeed. There is no doubt that the great mass of the civil service are exceedingly well qualified, a great many of them having superior qualifications ; and I am free to admit that, as a class, they do not deserve the attacks which are very often made upon them. At the same time. I think we -must all admit that there is a large -amount of work done by the service which is largely clerical-work which does not require -any special qualifications. That work is now done -chiefly by third-class clerks. The objection to -the present system is this, that when a young -man enters the civil service, he secures, -in nine cases out of ten, h-is permanent appointment as a third-class clerk ; he knows that during good conduct his position is permanent ; and, therefore, he has no-t that incentive to lay broad foundations for a successful future which a man has who knows that his permanency in the service depends on the manner in which he qualifies himself for the future service by -the -earlier years of his work.
He there takes the ground that appointments below the rank of the second-class, Which be does not disturb, should be temporary, so that the temporary nature of their employment might prove an incentive to them to win for themselves higher prizes In the civil service. On that occasion Sir Wilfrid Laurler, the leader of the opposition, expressed his objections to the Bill as follows :
This Bill is very objectionable in many ways. It provides for the abolition of third-class c'erks. The officers now employed as third-class clerks are to be maintained, but no new appointments are to be made to that class which henceforth i-s to be abolished. These employees are to be replaced by temporary clerks to be appointed at the w-ill of the -minister and the Governor in Council. The Bill proposed is calculated to lower itme character of the civil service. At present the clerk who is appointed to -the third class has a position in the department. He is not re-m-ovabale at the will -of the minister, but in the case of the lew officer, he is altogether dependent on the will of the minister. If ho is not like mitty in the hands of the head of the department he can be removed at will. He has no status whatever. It is of the greatest importance to the civil service that its members should have a Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
civil status. The hon. gentleman says that now the civil service have no Incentive to -do better.
It seems to -me the reverse is the oa33....
In my humble judgment this Bill is calculated to degrade the character of the civil service. It is very injudicious and most impolitic. The character of the service for efficiency ought to be maintained at the highest level, but this will be -removed if you take away from It the permanency now enjoyed and put it in the hands of -the minister to employ more writers whom they can discharge and replace at their own sweet will. I beg to move that the Bill be not now read the second -time brat that it be read the second time this day six months.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier was followed by Mr. McMullen, who also objected to the measure.
Wbat were the grounds of his objection ?

I have not read the whole of his argument, but my bon. friend will find it on page 3742. He was followed by Mr. Mills ; and the next and last speaker upon the question was the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) who X understand fills the position of leader of the Ontario opposition in this House to-day. He said :
I think there is a good deal of merit in the Bill proposed bv (the hon. Secretary of State, if the object -of this Bill is ito get efficient work done and pay a fair price for it. It does not seem to me there is anything objectionable in it, because it provides for geting the work done equally as well as it is done to-day ; but in addition to that it provides for making a great saving (to the country. Hon. gentlemen on the opposite benches generally complain when there is anything like over-expenditure or extravagance. Now, this Bill, makes for economy, and I (think they, at least, should support -it. Looking cursorily over the estimates, I find there are 320 third-class clerks in the service to-day.
If these 320 reach the maximum of the salary, that they could get under the present law, it means -a toal amount of $320,000 which -would have to be paid them aanuall* The maximum of that class is $1,000, and each of them will aim at reaching it, and as soon as they reach it they will be entitled to that salary. Many of them will exert pressure to be put into the next higher class, so that file man who reaches the next class, will still go on by statutory increase until he gets a larger salary. And yet the work is largely the same in both classes. The work is of a routine nature, and it might be done by any good writer or copyist. Now, then, why should we not save -this money if we can ? If we can get the work done quite as well by men who start at $400 a year and who can go no higher than $600 why should we commence lat $500 a ear, increasing the salary by $50 a ye-ar until they reach $1,000 ? If we take the 320 third-class clerk? who are employed, it would mean a saving every year of over $128,100 in the inside service, and that surely is a consideration that should weigh w-i-th this House, if it does not ia any way prevent the work from being done as -well as it is done now, and I believe it will be done quite as well.
Further on, he says :
I think we have too many classes ; we have a third class, a second class, and a fi-rst_ class, and then we have chief clerkships. This pro-

vision seems to have been made for the purpose of making more positions, to which big salaries are attached.
Two reasons were assigned for the abolition of the third class. One was that it did away with permanency and the other was the argument advanced by the hon. member for East Grey that it would make an economy of $400 per head on each person appointed to do the work, who, under the measure then submitted would only be able to reach a maximum of $600, whereas if the third class had been continued he would reach the higher maximum. The third class, at ail events, was abolished, and we think it should be restored to the extent to which we are restoring it. Since its abolition the present government established an additional class, the junior second, which filled up the hiatus between $600 and $1,000 the clerks entering at $600 and advancing to $1,000. This Bill proposes to restore the third class, the minimum being $500 and the maximum being $700. I am sure this will be a boon to a very large number, and I doubt if any provision in the Bill will bring greater benefits to a class more needing them.
Will this apply to the House of Commoons staff ?
No, the Civil Service Act does not apjply to the House of Commons or the Senate.
Why should it not be applied to them ? Would it not be better to place them under the Act than have them depending on the good-will of politicians ?

Referring to the suggestion of the hon. gentleman from Ottawa (Mr. Birkett), I think we ought not to take up any scheme that would lead to the postponement of this measure. If he seriously desires his proposition to be carried' into effect, I will snb-mit it to the government, but he will have to take the full responsibility of what that will involve.

I am sorry that the hon. the Postmaster General should take that view of the suggestion I made. That was not the spirit in which I made it. 1 have said that I approve of the Bill, but what I desired was that every one in the departments should have his case provided for. The suggestion I made was on behalf of those who are not included in the Bill, and will not get any benefit from it. It was merely a verbal suggestion, which I had afterwards prepared hurriedly in typewriting ; and if defective in any particular, I should be most hapipy to have it amended. I understand that the session is too far advanced for the government or the House, perhaps, to go beyond the present measure, and I have no intention of offering it any opposition, but on the contrary, give it every support. But what I desire is that the 392J
government should during recess consider the proposition I have submitted and devise a measure which will deal justly with those who are not dealt with in the present one. It is not my purpose or desire to take any credit to myself in this matter, although I think I was the first to submit the figures and the suggestions which the government have partially dealt with. The honourable the senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt)' -whether he be the senior or not is a matter of no import-seems anxious to take every; opportunity of assuming credit for this measure. So far as I am personally concerned, as I said the other evening, he is at perfect liberty to take all the credit. I have no desire to make any political capital out of it, nor has anybody on this side, although every attempt has been made in that direction by the senior member. All I want is to have justice meted out as much as possible towards all the members of the civil service. In that spirit, I would suggest that the Bill be accepted in its present shape and that the government should, during the recess, consider the advisability of bringing down next session a larger measure, which would deal out uniform fairness to all concerned.

My hon. friend has somewhat cleared the atmosphere. He tells us that his suggestion was hardly prepared with that care he would like to have given it, and he would desire to have it interpreted in the light of the remarks be has just made. I will so interpret it, although it is otpen to the other interpretation, that he desired a committee to make a complete revision and asked the government to appoint a committee to inquire of the heads of the departments as to the work and salary of all members of the staff, temporary and permanent, for the purpose of making a complete and uniform revision of the Civil Service, including those for whom we are now legislating, as well as others. However, my hon. friend takes another view, and I will take his suggestion to be that we should in the recess consider this question.
Deal with the balance of the departments.

I understand it now. We will tak* it that way that we shall in the recess consider any part of the work that is now left unfinished with a view to further action. Thus we clear the atmosphere and my hon. friend gives his approval to the measure as far as it goes.
Yes, I do.

The Postmaster General suggested that my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) was endeavouring in some way to obstruct this Bill. I did not gather that the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) was doing anything of the kind ; I understood in the first place that
12511)

he had made suggestions which had been acted upon by the Postmaster General. That certainly shows that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Birkett) was not attempting to obstruct the Bill in any way, but, on the other hand has been endeavouring to assist the government in working out a scheme which will do justice to the employees. The suggestion of the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) simply amounts to this, that he wants the Bill to go further ; he distinctly said in his remarks that the Postmaster General was on the right road and was doing right.
Undoing what was done in 18S5.
My hon. friend cannot get the political question out of his head.
We are doing right. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) is the only perfect statesman.
I was endeavouring to discuss this Bill apart from political questions.
We are ail doing that

And to point out that the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) suggested that, as the Bill in its present shape is not sufficiently comprehensive, a committee of some kind might be appointed to consider all questions connected with the civil service and in that way enable the government to bring in at a future session, or during this session if time permitted, some measure which would deal with certain anomalies that still exist. Some question has been raised with regard to the scope of these resolutions, particularly with regard to the scope of those officers more immediately under the control of the House of Commons, of whom there are a very considerable number. I suppose their cases may demand some consideration. I am not very fully informed as to the exact position of members of the staff, but I know that a great many very capable and efficient officers are under the control of the House: the librarians of parliament, for example, are under the control of a joint committee of the Senate and the House or of the commissioners on internal economy, and I would ask if there is anything in this measure with regard to them as well as to the other officers similarly placed. If the hon. Postmaster General would give us his views with regard to these officers it might be of some service to us in considering the proposition made in the Bill.

The Bill states plainly the parties to whom it applies. It applies to the class of deputy heads, which would carry with it all persons holding the rank of deputy head, it applies to chief clerks, first-class clerks, second-class

clerks, junior second-class clerks, temporary Writers, temporary clerks, messengers, porters, packers and sorters in the inside service. But we all know there are many classes in the service inside and outside in addition to those I have enumerated, and many of them doubtless have claims for recognition and may receive increases. The joint librarians of parliament are yery valuable officers, but the question of salary, per se, is a matter for supply rather than for a measure of this kind which creates a new class or deals with the salaries of existing classes. I do not know that the librarians are placed with any general class, but, I think, they are unique officers. Perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) is aware how that Is ; I really do not.
I do not know, I am asking for information.

I think they stand alone and that they are not classed ; they are special officers. Mr. Speaker informs me they have a status given to them by a special Act and that any increases in their salary should be properly dealt with in the estimates and would not properly fall within the provisions of a measure of this kind dealing with the civil service.
How are the salaries of the librarians and other officers of the Senate and the House of Commons fixed ?

There is an anomaly about that; my impression is that some of the employees in the library belong to the classes and I dare say that this measure will apply to some of them. But the librarians themselves are special officers not brought under any class. Their present salary which is fixed by the statute is, I think, $3,200.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot agree with the statement of the Postmaster General that this is a very meritorious Act. It contains too many blemishes, too many serious defects to be at all meritorious. The evident desire of the Postmaster General is to get as many of the civil servants as possible under the absolute control of the government. The hon. gentleman (Sir Wm. Mulock) cannot see anything except the political side of it, he is so imbued with the political idea that he must make everything serve his political desires and his political objects. This whole Bill shows a desire to get control of the civil service so that the salaries will be under control of the government. That is one of its most serious defects and the hon. gentleman_ calls it rectifying what was done in 1895. Is he abolishing temporary clerks or doing away with temporary service ? Not by any means. What wrong does he rectify ? We have already established a class of junior

second-class clerks. If there is any rectification of a wrong, that class of junior second-class clerks will take that of the third-class clerks that they abolished in 1895. The hon. gentleman is running up against the very thing that was pointed out by one of his friends in this debate of 1S95, in a statement that was made by Mr. Mills, afterwards a minister in this cabinet. At page 3766 of the ' Hansard,' Mr. Mills says :
This is a proposition to exeroiee a dispensing power.
I invite the hon. gentleman's attention to this language of his late colleague :
Of course, there are always favourites or proteges of the administration or of its supporters, for whom it is necessary to make special provision. They do not belong to the vulgar herd who are obliged to go up in regular order and submit themselves for examination.
Now there is a provision here that there shall be no examination with respect to certain persons, on the recommendation of the head of the department, the political head. On his recommendation, certain persons will be allowed to go back to the third-class, under this Bill, without examination.
How many political heads of the department are political friends of the government just now ?

There is one political head right in front of the hon. gentleman, for instance. I do not know what sort of deputy head there is alongside of him at this moment. An hon. gentleman suggests that the Postmaster General is double-headed because he is Minister of Labour.
Now, Mr. Mills goes on to say :
They do not belong to the vulgar herd who are obliged to go up in regular order and submit themselves for examination. It would be grossly unfair to treat them as ordinary mortals. Qualification is not as important in their case as it might be in the case of others. A little ignorance will do them no harm ; a little incompetency on their part is no disadvantage to the public service. It is only necessary that the government should have a dispensing power in order that those persons, whether qualified to do the work or not, whether capable of passing an examination or not may be promoted.
Now, if that language was applicable in 1895, it is still more applicable to-day, and I would commend that language of Mr. Mills to the hon. gentlemen opposite. It was used in the very same debate from which the hon. gentleman was reading an extract, though he took good care not to read this particular extract, because Mr. Mills' language at that time would not suit him on this present occasion.
At one o'clock, committee took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.

Before the discussion upon these resolutions ends I wish to remind the hon. Postmaster General that a deputation from some of the clerks
representing the outside service waited upon him some months ago and laid before him their case as contrasted with the case of the inside service. In so far as I can judge upon that occasion the clerks who represented the interests of the outside men made a very strong case indeed from their point of view, and I understood the hon. Postmaster General was going to take into consideration what was said by them. As I recollect the matter it was put in this way : That the outside men, while they may have been in the departments for as many years as gentlemen in the inside service, are not allowed the same salaries although they have longer hours to work, more hours in the week, and not only frequently have to perform night service, but occasionally have to work on Sundays. I do not know that there should be any distinction between the two services. Certainly there was nothing said on that occasion either by the hon. gentleman or,by any person speaking on behalf of the men that indicated why there ought to be any difference. The only inference I can draw from the one set of men being dealt with now and not the other is that probably the men in the inside service have better means of bringing their case to the attention of the government than the others, and I should hope that the hon. Postmaster General, in view of the suggestion made by my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Birlcett), would take the cases of the outside men into consideration and endeavour to do them full justice. I understand from what the hon. minister has said that already this session there has been a change made in their compensation, and that this has advanced them in some degree, but I do not think it meets the whole point. The question is not so much whether the outside men have had an increase of their salaries as whether the complaint they made that they were not treated on the same footing as men of equal rank in the inside service has been met. It seems to me that they are entitled to as much consideration from the government as the others. I mention that particularly now because of the very business-like and sensible suggestion made by my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) that	after	the passage of
this Bill the whole subject of the increases in the salaries of the civil service in connection with the various departments, not only the Post Office Department, but of all the civil service, be taken up and dealt with by a committee, so that we may have a report upon the whole subject next session. I cannot imagine anything more likely to do justice all round than that suggestion, and I may say here that it was with some surprise that I heard the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) express an objection to the proposal or suggestion made by my hon. friend (Mr. Birkett). I can only say for myself that I

believe If that liappy thought had occurred to the hon. gentleman opposite he would have proposed it himself. He would have thought it a most admirable one. but I fear he has opposed it simply because the suggestion came from this side of the House. X am sorry that the hon. Postmaster General should take the suggestion in rather a critical manner. The suggestion was made in good spirit. My hon. friend from Ottawa did not profess to have carefully drawn a motion. He merely wrote on the spur of the moment the suggestion, and if that suggestion was taken in the spirit in which it was made I think it would be to the advantage of the service and to all concerned. I shall be very glad indeed if his suggestion be received and acted upon by the minister. I think that by what has been said by the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) he also is now disposed, and I think he should be disposed, to accept it in the spirit in which it was proposed by my hon. friend.

I stated to the committee before one o'clock that I was quite prepared to accept the qualification expressed by the hon. member for Ot-awa (Mr. Birkett) in regard to the suggestion which he made, although the suggestion was not fairly open to the particular interpretation which he desired to place upon it. I do not desire to make any point of that, although I would tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) that the suggestion which the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) made was not a hastily scribbled suggestion, but was in typewriting and evidently had been carefully considered. But, let that go. We can all make mistakes, and I am not disposed to press the point at all. But, let us try to keep the facts in view. There is a difference between the salaries paid the outside and inside service. If we compare them man for man according to the classes in which they are, there is a different amount assigned to a clerkship in the outside service from what there is assigned to a clerkship in the inside service. I do not know why that has been so. It is not of to-day's creation. I think it has always been so, and I am pleased to find that our hon. friends of the opposition are so much more willing to come to the relief of the civil service than they were when they had an opportunity of being of practical benefit tc them. We were considering at one o'clock the question of the third class, and that is the subject now engaging the attention of the committee. It is possible to go into the whole range of the civil service. In reference to the deputation to which my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) refers, probably what I have said to some extent deals with that question, but, however that may be, I only repeat that the government has in all its legislation affecting the civil service moved in the direction of bettering their position. We have in the past made some progress.

We are making more progress to-day, and the progress we are making, if this measure is allowed to pass, added to what we have done, will, I think, fairly indicate the policy of the government in regard to the civil service. There is a number of classes yet to be dealt with. I trust that their time will come.

Mr. Chairman, I do not profess to defend the conduct of any political party in the past. It takes about all the time I can give to my duties to attend to present affairs. All I can say is that I cannot understand why a gentleman occupying a position in the post office on one side of the street, living in the same city and subject to the same expenses, should have a lower wage than a gentleman on rhe other side of the same street. It does seem to me that the reasons which were brought before the hon. Postmaster General by the deputation to which I referred, that these gentlemen had longer hours in the post office, that they had night service and that they had Sunday service, ought to have influenced the hon. minister in making the salaries more nearly alike. In regard to what I said as to my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Birkett), I can only say that I listened to what he said when he read his suggestion to the minister, and I distinctly understood him, and I doubt whether any person in this House could fail to understand him, to say that he approved of the Bill before the committee as far as it goes. He desired not to obstruct the Bill, nor to prevent it from passing, but that at the earliest possible moment the whole subject should be considered by the committee that he suggested. Whether he had prepared his suggestion in typewriting or not is of no importance. It is obvious to everybody that he meant that the Bill now before the committee should not be opposed, but that the whole subject should be dealt with at the earliest possible moment.

The impression created on my mind by the statement of any hon. colleague (Mr. Birkett) this morning was that he asked to have this matter investigated by a committee of gentlemen, who would wait on the deputy heads and ascertain their opinion as to the temporary clerks in the different departments of the service. That was evidently the impression created on the mind of the Postmaster General also. The result of that suggestion would have been to defer the consideration of this Bill indefinitely and very probably it would prevent the Bill passing at the present session. My hon. friend (Mr. Birkett) afterwards explained that he intended that the investigation should take place during the recess, and the report submitted during the next session. It is unnecessary for me to say that I agree with him to that extent, because when I spoke on this matter the other

night that was one of the several suggestions which I submitted to the consideration of the government. I then asked that the case of the technical and temporary officers in Customs, Interior, Railways and Canals and Public Works Departments should be investigated, and ample provision made for them. I also referred to a certain number of gentlemen who are dioing clerical work, particularly in the Department of Public Works ; in fact, I repeated that suggestion this morning before my hon. friend (Mr. Birkett) spoke at all. Therefore, when his suggestion takes the shape that there may be an investigation during the recess and a report submitted early next session, I thoroughly agree with it. However, I do not think it- is necessary that a committee of members, or a committee of other persons should toe appointed for that purpose. It seems to me that the executive of the different departments will be able to look into the matter and make a report themselves. My hon. colleague (Mr. Birkett) did not intimate what kind of a committee he wanted, but at any rate I do not think it necessary to have a committee, as the heads of the department and the members of the Council will toe able to discharge that duty themselves. I rose for the purpose of correcting the impression which my hon. friend is trying to create, namely, that I am opposed to the members of the government investigating the matter. I am not opposed to that at all, but I am opposed to any suggestion which will delay the consideration of the Bill at this stage, because I fear very much that if the Bill is not passed now there will be no measure of relief for the civil servants this year and possibly not next year. For that reason, I am most anxious that nothing should toe done that would in any way delay the passage of this measure.

We have been in session for six and a-half months, and it is'strange what tremendous haste there is about this Bill now. Why did not the hon. member (Mr. Beicourt) prevail on his friend the Postmaster General and Minister of Labour to bring this Bill forward at an early date, and make it cover all classes of the service?
We have it now, and let us deal with it.

We have a Bill now which only affords a very small measure of relief to the civil servants. I was rather surprised-no, I take that back, because nothing that the Postmaster General would do would surprise any one. But it is amusing to hear the Minister of Labour stand up now and pose as the friend of the civil servants. He forgets that since his government came into power they deprived a very large number of -the civil servants of the statutory increases which they were entitled to in the years 1S97, 189S and 1899, at a loss to each civil servant of several hundred dollars. That is what the Liberal government has done for the civil servants, and now the Postmaster General attempts to pose as their friend. In his intense desire for economy along certain lines, forgetful of the extravagance he and his colleagues were guilty of along certain other lines, an extravagance which far outweighed the little economy they were able to practice by robbing the civil servants who wrere 'entitled to this statutory increase. He robbed these servants of two or three hundred dollars each, and then wasted it upon favourite contractors and others. I stated this morning that one great objection to the present Bill was that it threw too much power into the hands of the heads of the departments. That was the contention made by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were on this side of the House, in 1895. I will read from ' Hansard ' of 1895, an extract from a speech made toy a very prominent Liberal, who said :
There is another objection to this proposal. This increase is not to he statutory, as it is now in the case of what I may call the covenant civil servants, but it is to be at the pleasure of the deputy heads, endorsed by the head of the department.
That was the proposition made in 1895, which secured the endorsation of the Liberal party at that time. They now say they are going to give a measure of relief to the civil servants, but what they are doing is to continue the bad practice of their predecessors instead of improving on it. I again quote :
That practically means that the head of the department, who is the supreme master of the patronage.
Let me call the attention of the Postmaster General to the fact that this is the declaration by one of his colleagues who was in the House at that time :
That practically means that ithe head of the department, who Is the supreme master of the patronage, twill be allowed to add thirty dollars a year to the salary of those whom he favours

The only difference now is that this is an increase of fifty dollars instead of thirty dollars, and it gives the head of the department all the bigger pull upon the civil servant.
-and to not add it to the salary of those whom he does not favour. I object entirely to the practice of leaving the extra pay to the head of the department.
That was said by a very prominent member of the Liberal party in 1895, who is not now in the House. I especially call the attention of the Tostmaster General to that language, and I remind him that that very serious defect exists in this Bill. It has another very serious defect. It gives no immediate relief to the civil servants. It is like the National Transcontinental Railway, which will not relieve the congestion of traffic for eight or ten years to come. The relief that is to be given by tbis Bill has

to be waited for, and it only affects two or three classes of public servants. The man who is just joining the service gets a little higher salary than he could otherwise, and it slightly betters the position of those who are promoted from being messengers and sorters to the position of third-class clerks.
Does it take in letter-carriers ?
No doubt, that worries you very much.

I am sure that my hon. friend (Mr. Belcourt) is altogether too high-minded to consider the question of making political capital, but anyhow he will find that what I say is correct. There should have been a levelling up of these salaries, or a levelling down if you like, and that should be done on the percentage basis. Why should the man at the head of the list receive an increase of 25 per cent, while the man at the foot of the list only gets five per cent increase ? Do you mean to tell me that the expenses of a man receiving $500 or $600 a year have not proportionately increased with those of the man receiving $4,000 ? Look what the poor man has to pay for fuel and for everything else that he uses ; the cost has increased at least twenty-five or thirty per cent during the past eight or ten years. But you only increase his salary five per cent, while you increase the salary of the man at the head of the list twenty-five per cent. It seems to me that that is absolutely unfair. If a man is receiving two dollars a day, give him an increase of twenty-five per cent and then he will receive $2.50. That need not interfere with your increasing a salary of $4,000 to $5,000 a year. I do not say that the mani at the head of the department should not have his salary increased. If he was entitled to a salary of $4,000 thirty years ago, he is entitled to a salary of $5,-

000 low, because the expenses of living have very much increased. But that scale of increase applies to the man with the small salary as well as to the man with the high salary. The Postmaster General has already revised this Bill once, and now that he has received some light on the subject and has had the advantage of the criticism from this side of the House, let him withdraw this resolution as he withdrew the former one, and let him go to work and revise this Bill. The hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) need not fear that there will not be plenty of time to do this. We will be here for three or four weeks yet, and the Postmaster General will have ample time to prepare a measure which will deal out justice to all classes in the service. That is what we on this side of the House ask. We do not believe in cheese-paring with respect to these matters. We believe in paying a man a fair day's pay for a fail-day's work. No man on this side of the House will object to that. We will not pursue the tactics which the Liberals pursued when they were in opposition. We have no such small critics among us as the Postmaster General, who was one of the worst offenders in that respect when he sat in opposition. We want to see that the right class of men are employed in the civil service, and then we want them paid fair wages. We want the increase in their salaries to be statutory, so that it will not depend upon the whim of the gentleman who happens to be at the head of the department for the time being. We want the increase in salary statutory so that a man will not have to make his politics conform to the politics of the minister in order that he may get fair play and justice. Therefore, I say, that if the Postmaster General really wants to bring forward a fair measure for the relief of the civil service-and I have my doubts about that-the best thing he can do is to withdraw this resolution, and replace it by another which will accord that due measure of relief to which these gentlemen are entitled.
On section 11, salary of third-class clerk.

Before this clause is adopted, I wish to ask the Minister of Labour, or some other minister, if they will announce the intention of the government with respect to the recommendation of the Senate committee, to which I have referred ?

I thought perhaps my hon. friend was familiar with the rule in regard to the privilege of parliament. The salaries of the officers of the Senate and House of Commons are really determinable by those two bodies. Of course, technically the government of the day can refuse assent to recommendations for increase of salary ; but it has never been the practice of either the English parliament, the mother of parliaments, or of this parliament for the government of the day to take the initiative in determining the salaries of the officers of parliament. The question of the payment of the officers of the two Houses is regarded as a question of privilege, and no doubt that is the reason why the officers of the House and the Senate have been excluded from the provisions of all Civil Service Acts since 1872. All officers who are provided for by this Act are officers of the government; their appointment, their salaries and their dismissal are under the control of the government ; but the appointment, salaries and dismissals of officers of the House and the Senate rests with practically those bodies themselves.

I quite understand that; but the hon. gentleman has not answered the question. He takes the position, which I understood to be the rule and custom, that the salaries of officers of the Senate may be increased by the Senate; but those increases are subject to the revision of the government, and the government can say whether they w... assent to them or not. The government have control of the public treasury, out of which these salaries must be paid, and they cannot be paid unless the government give their assent. What I ask is whether it is the. intention of the government to assent to these increases ; because, if so, we must see to it that the salaries of the officers of the House of Commons are increased in the same proportion. The government would not assent to the proposition unless they considered it a reasonable one, and it would not be reasonable for the officials of the House of Commons to be paid less than the officials of the Senate.
On section 14-transfer of writer, clerk, packer, sorter, or messenger to a third-class clerkship.

Before this is carried, I would like to make a further suggestion, but in no way to interfere with the passage of the present Bill this session. I would like that to be understood if I make a suggestion. I would suggest to the hon. Postmaster General that he provide that all temporary writers who have been in the employ of the government for a period of fifteen years or over in continuous service, at the time of the coming into force of this Act, and who have performed their duty to the satisfaction of the head of the department, shall receive the maximum salary of their class provided by this Act.
X presume that my hon. friend is not serious in making the motion, for he has already learned that no private member can make a motion/ that involves an increase of expenditure.
Can he make a suggestion ?

If that suggestion were to be acquiesced in by the

government, it would involve the suspension of this measure until the proposition could be submitted to His Excellency and his assent obtained.
That would not be a very serious matter. It would not involve a delay of more than twfenty-four hours.
I do not know how many hours of delay it would involve. I do not know how many suggestions we would have to take up. There are a sheaf of them.
That shows how imperfect your Bill is.
My hon. friends have the choice of opposing the Bill or approving of it.

I do not think it is proper for the hon. Postmaster General to make a remark of that kind. It is perfectly proper for hon. gentlemen on this side of the House to make suggestions with reference to these resolutions, and I do not think such a remark from the hon.
