Postmaster General would prevent any one on this side of the House from doing that. I do not supppose the attitude of the hon. gentleman is that we must regard the resolutions as perfect, on the penalty of having it withdrawn. The proposed Bill may be possible to make it a great deal better ; but we are not, I suppose, to be constrained by the threat that if we make a suggestion in this committee, the hon. gentleman may withdraw his Bill. That is hardly the attitude my hon. friend would like to assume. I imagine. He is responsible for this measure, I imagine. He is responsible for this measure, and every member of this House is responsible for doing what he can to improve it. The suggestion which my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) has made would seem to me to be a very good one.

It is rather inconsistent, too, I think, for the hon. Postmaster General, the Minister of Labour, to take that position. This is not the first civil service amendment Bill which has been introduced this session. It is the second one, and it is largely based on suggestions made by the hon. member (or Ottawa (Mr. Birkett). If that hon. gentleman thinks it his duty to offer some further suggestions, surely he should not be threatened with the withdrawal of the Bill altogether. I think his suggestions are timely. and I hope the minister will take them into his consideration, and make further amendments to the Bill before it is finally passed.
On section 15-customs schedule,
Will the hon. gentleman tell us what the changes are ?
I will read the changes I understand this schedule to make. They are as follows :

Tide waiters, under the old law, went from $800 to $1,000. Under this resolution they will go from $800 to $1,200. Lockers, under the old law, went as high as $S00. Under this resolution they will go from $400 to $1,000. Packers, under the old law, went to $500 ; under this resolution they will go to $600. Messengers had, under the old law, a maximum of $500 and began at $200. Under this law the minimum will be $300 and the maximum $600. Tide waiters, under the old law, went to $500. Under this law they will go from $400 to $600.

Let me draw attention to another disparity. The door-keeper of the Senate receives a salary of $950 and the door-keeper of the House of Commons gets only $480, although he has much more work to do. Does the government propose to assent to this ? If it does, it will be incumbent on the House of Commons to take some step to bring the salary of its door-keeper within a measurable distance of that of the door-keeper of the Senate.
It will be for the committee of this House to take any action it sees proper. The privileges of this House are under its control.
How can the hon. gentleman account for the disparity in the salaries ?
The salaries paid in the Senate are largely decided by the Senate Committee and those paid in the House of Commons are decided by the Commons Committee.

A number of men have been passed over the heads of other men in the various departments, and this has been done by voting them increased amounts, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act to the contrary. Are these men to have the advantages of the increases under this resolution and thus get double increases ?
The PbSTMASTER GENERAL. If this resolution should go through, the government will then be empowered to deal with the different officers who' come within its provisions. Take my own department, it will be the duty of the deputy minister to decide what officers are entitled to an increase. If his report is approved by the minister, it will be submitted to the council, and if approved by council it will go into effect. It has always been the practice for the government to pass an Order in Council deciding whether or not increases shall take place and that practice will not be departed from. As the maximum of each class has been increased, the government will have more scope to increase the salaries. I do not know to what cases my hon. friend refers when he speaks of officers having been promoted over the heads of others. I do not think he could make that charge with regard to my department.

A number of such instances were brought to the attention of the gov-

eminent and speeches made on this side protesting against the practice. Under these resolutions every one of these men will benefit by the increase. They will doubly benefit-in the first place by their promotion over the heads of others and in the second place by getting the increases provided in these, resolutions, whereas the men they have passed over will remain as they are. I understood the hon. minister to say that he wished to benefit all branches. That is what we want done ; and I do not find that the hon. gentleman has met the question I put him.

I assure my hon. friend (Mr. Boyd) that I do not wish to evade the question. He will find that under this measure no one can get an increase until the time elapses which authorizes the increase. If some person has been pitchforked over the heads of others this session I have not heard of it.
On section 16-Inland Revenue schedule.

The following are the changes under this section : The office of chief inspector is abolished. The maximum salary of a collector is increased from $2,200 to $2,400; of a deputy collector, from $1,500 to $1,700; of an accountant, from $1,400 to $1,500; of special class excise men, from $1,600 to $1,800; of other special class excise men from $1,200 to $1,400; of first, second and third-class excise men, from $1,000 to $1,200. In the salaries of messengers, the minimum, now $200, is increased to $400 and the maximum, now $500, is increased to $700. Then there is a new class added, stenographers, minimum $400 and maximum $600 ?
Are the inspectors in the Inland Revenue Department inspectors of distilleries or of gas, electric light, &c. ?

You have not been in the House or you would have heard of it.
These are the inspectors for divisions.

If such a case exists it will not entitle any person to an increase until the time has elapsed which entitled him to it. Of course there may be cases in which there are special reasons why a person would be treated specially. If my hon. friend (Mr. Boyd) was in a position of responsibility on the government side he would find that ministers are not as bad as he now thinks us and that what may seem to be injustice is not so in fact. For instance a case was brought to my attention to-day which I would call to the attention of my hon. friend and ask how he would deal with it. It is not a case coming up to be dealt with, but it struck me as a very hard case indeed. This man, a messenger, entered the service in 1871, but he was not placed on the permanent list, owing to an oversight, until 1892.
Was it Professor Pope ?
They take the position of chief inspector ?
No, that position is abolished. We have inspectors for divisions. There are three or four in Ontario and three or four in Quebec.
The office of chief inspector has been abolished and that position is now filled by a divisional inspector. Is that correct ?
Yes.

Will the Minister of Inland Revenue tell me how it is that deputy collectors of Inland revenue do not receive in their class a maximum salary equal to that paid to some of the excisemen ? The special officer class can reach $2,000 while the deputy collector can reach only $1,400. Is the deputy collector inferior to the excisemen ?
No. It was not Professor Pope. Now, that is a very hard case, is it not ?
Yes, it seems to be.

If it were not too late I might ask that it be considered but that case may have to be dealt with later on and in that event on the surface it would look as if that man was being treated in a special way ? There may be cases of that kind that appear to be exceptional or partisan but which are not so in fact. If the hon. gentleman analyzes all these special cases he will find a fair and reasonable explanation for most of them.
Might I ask if the salaries of technical officers, the appraisers in the customs department, have been changed ?
No, that is the same, $800 to $2,000.

The deputy collector is not in either class A or B and is not bound to pass any examination. His responsibility as deputy collector is less than that of an officer who has charge of a distillery for instance. These officers who are in charge of distilleries must pass first the qualifying examination and then a promotion examination, afterwards passing special examinations. The special class excisemen are limited to the number of twenty-four. These have charge of the distilleries for the Dominion. The salary of a deputy collector is smaller because his responsibility is less than that of the special class excise man.
I do not know whether it is germane to this discussion but I would like to ask the Minister of Inland Revenue if any suggestions have been made to him as to the appointment of official weighers ?
These officers no longer belong to my department. They are under the Department of Trade and Commerce.

I have a letter which begins :
The Toronto Board ot Trade and the Dominion Millers' Association have both passed strong resolutions asking the government to appoint sworn official weighers at the various public elevators this side of the lakes, to be paid by fee so that no expense will be entailed on the government.

There is authority under the Manitoba Grain Inspection Act to appoint such officers, but there is no authority to appoint them elsewhere. However, I have that matter at this present moment under consideration, amd I may possibly have to introduce an amendment to the General Inspection Act giving power to appoint these officers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) is seized of the fact that there is a desire on the part of the board of trade to have these special officers ?

The matter is being investigated at this moment, and while I do not wish to introduce contentious measures at this period of the session, still, if the general sense of the House is that this legislation is desirable, we may have an amendment to the Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
The letter of the Toronto Board of Trade is as follows :
The Toronto Board of Trade and the Dominion Millers' Association have both passed strong resolutions asking the government to appoint sworn official weighers at the various public elevators this .side of the lakes, to be paid by fee so that no expense will be entailed on the government. The millers have suffered very heavy losses for years back owing to shortage of grain arriving from lake elevators, and as the government appointment of official weighers at Fort William and Port Arthur has apparently given satisfaction to both the shippers and receivers we feel that the appointment of sworn weighers at Sarnia, Goderich, Owen Sound, Midland, Meafoird, Parry Sound and such other points where the fees would be sufficient to secure the services of a thoroughly competent man, would be of great benefit and satisfaction to all concerned.
We have no authority at the present moment to act east of the lakes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
You might take it. There would be no factious opposition.
On paragraph 17,

Might I ask the Minister of Customs what increases are contemplated to be given in Prince Edward Island to the officials in his department under this law ? I would also ask the Minister of Inland Revenue if he contemplates giving increases to his officials ?

I do not know whether any increases have been granted this year or not, there are some under consideration. I could not inform the hon. gentleman off-hand what increases will be given in the outside service. In that service the salaries do not go up as a matter of course ; the increase is granted upon merit, taking each case individually.

I have here a copy of the Charlottetown ' Patriot,' the organ of the government in the province of Prince Edward Island. I find an editorial in that paper dated September 18th, under the heading ' Good news to all.'
The news in to-day's despatches is sufficiently startling even for those who believe that there is nothing new under the sun. In the first place there is good news from Ottawa-something that will cause thousands of civil service officials in, Canada, their wives and families, as well as storekeepers and a host of others-indeed, the public at large-to rejoice. According to the announcement of the resolution of which Sir William Mulock has given notice in parliament, it provides for an increase in the salaries of all officials from Deputy Ministers down to sorters and packers in the entire civil service.
That sounds like elections.

Yes. I would like to ask the minister if it is the intention to increase the salaries of the customs officials, and the post office officials, and the inland revenue officials in the province of Prince Edward Island, by this Act, or has this editorial been inserted in the government organ in Charlottetown for the purpose of deceiving the civil service in the province of Prince Edward Island ?

Well, I would hesitate to imply anything like that. I suppose that parties form their own inference when they see on the paper notices of a resolution, and evidently that impression has been formed by the correspondent of that paper. The Bill of the Postmaster General, however, refers to the inside service at Ottawa. So far as the outside service of the Customs Department is concerned, it makes a change in the way of grouping the officials more than they have been before, and defining their salaries, but their salaries remain about as they were before. But the hon. gentleman will notice that there is quite a difference between the minimum and maximum salary fixed there. In the outside service of the Customs Department the increases are not given automatically, they are given according to merit, and each ease is dealt with individually. We have during the past year recognized that many of the civil servants in the outside service, owing to changed conditions and enhanced cost of living, were deserving of more than they have hitherto been receiving. In the case of others we have not seen our way clear to advance their salaries.

Still others are under consideration at the present time, waiting the sanction of this Bill, and a vote that we may ask for in the supplementary estimates.
Does the minister mean to say that this Bill does not deal at all with the outside service of the Customs Department ?

It does not ideal with the outside service except in the way that I have alluded to, namely, in grouping certain classes of officials, but leaving the differences between the minimum and maximum much the same. In this measure temporary officers in the outside service that have not passed the civil service examination, will be admitted to the permanent list upon passing a practical examination, which will be held under papers prepared by the commissioner of the department. That is as far as the Bill will affect the outside customs service.
Then this statement in the paper that increases were to take place from the deputy minister down to sorters and packers in the entire civil service is entirely incorrect.
It is not incorrect so far as the inside service is concerned.
It says the ' entire civil service.'
It would not necessarily include the outside service, though we have in the outside service packers and messengers.
That is, the outside service is not dealt with in this Bill ?

The hon. gentleman will see in the resolution that the salary of a packer, whether in the outside or the inside service, may range from $300 to $600. All that section dealing with the customs has reference to the outside service as well as to the inside service.
I suppose it is only the officials of the inside who will really benefit ?
Not necessarily.
Men who are in the outside service get cold justice. Is there any provision made in this Bill at all for letter carriers throughout the Dominion, and country postmasters ?
I supposed the hon. gentleman is aware that letter carriers were dealt with by a measure passed this session, to which the hon. gentleman gave his hearty approval.

Possibly, in view of the fact that we have had the Dominion Trades and Labour Council at its recent meeting
making a pronunciamento with respect to this deserving class of officials, the hon. Minister of Labour may have considered it and may give us some intimation of what he intends doing. I am speaking to the hon. gentleman now as Minister of Labour.
I will take the matter into my serious consideration. I will call the attention of the Postmaster General to the matter.

I wish to say that I have been looking into the matter of the internal economy of this Efouse, and I find that it is under the control of commissioners, of whom the hon. Speaker is one. Estimates are prepared by the commissioners, submitted to the Minister of Finance and then come before the House. I would like to point out to the House and to impress upon the minds of the commissioners, some of whom I see present, the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright), the hon. Minister of Finance and the Speaker, the absolute necessity of equalizing the salaries paid on this side of parliament and the salaries paid on the other side-in the Senate. There is no reason in the world why a man on this side is not entitled to as much pay as a man on the Senate side. He is in fact entitled to a great deal more from the fact that his hours are a great deal longer and that the service he performs is very much greater. Take the matter of the clerks. There are two assistant clerks in the Senate, one of whom receives $2,800, and the other $1,800, or $2-000. In this House there is only one assistant clerk, who is in receipt of a salary of $2,200. It does seem to me that the disproportion is very great between the two. If the assistant clerk of this House is receiving a proper remuneration for the services which he has to perform then the two assistant clerks in the Senate are receiving a far greater remuneration than that to which they are entitled. That House does not sit one day out of twenty-I was going to say-certainly, not one hour out of twenty that this House sits, and the labour performed is infinitely less there than it is here. Then, the doorkeeper of the Senate receives $950 a year as against $500 paid to the doorkeeper of this House. I hojpe the commissioners will take this matter into their earnest consideration and see that a proper measure of fair-play Is afforded to the officers of this House.
If my hon. friend should be of the opinion that the officers of the Senate are paid too much should we make the matter still worse by adding to the salaries of the officers in the House of Commons ?
I did not express any opinion as to that.
The hon. gentleman wants to equalize it.

The officials on the other side of the House are asking now that their salaries shall be raised. Clearly the government has to say as to whether that shall be done or not under the British North America Act.
I think that is correct.

All matters affecting the expenditure of money must come before the Governor in Council, and he should have the right to say whether these salaries should be increased or not. Surely you are not going to allow the salaries which are much higher than the salaries paid to the officers of this House to be put still higher and leave the salaries of the officers here at the same figure ? Either the salaries on the Senate side are too high or the salaries on this side are too low. They should be equalized in some way. I am not expressing any opinion as to which it is. But, I think that the internal economy commissioners should consider this matter.
We find that there seems to be a disposition on the part of the Senate to go into a little more liberal expenditure than we do on this side.
The Senate is more Liberal now than it used to be.

Even under other administrations it has been the same. There seems to be something in the increased dignity of the other Chamber which renders it necessary that things should be done on a more generous scale. I largely agree with the hon. gentleman that there are inequalities in the matter.

How were these salaries fixed in the first instance and how are they dealt with now ? I understand from what the hon. Postmaster General said that committees of the House and Senate control the matter in some way. Is that the case or is the whole matter of salaries controlled by the commissioners of internal economy ? I hurriedly read the provisions of the statute but they do not seem to be very clear as to the authority which shall have charge of this matter.

We have on a great many occasions had reports from committees of this House. Take for example the ' Hansard ' and Printing committees. We have had reports recommending increases of salary for the ' Hansard ' reporters.
Who is the body which eventually determines these salaries ? Is it the House, or a committee of the House, or the commissioners appointed to manage the internal economy of the House ?
There are the internal economy commissioners in so far as the affairs of the House of Commons are concerned. They have nothing to

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: do with the Senate. In all cases the ultimate judgment is with the House of Commons, with the initiation of the government, because the moneys necessary have to be included in the estimates, so that theoretically the matter is in the hands of the government. However, there are limitations, as hon. gentlemen know, in practical politics. The Senate is very sensitive upon what it regards as its rights. It appoints committees to arrange the salaries of its officers, and while it has not power to control the matter it makes recommendations and it is very highly displeased if its recommendations are not granted. As a matter of theory the government controls the matter, but the theory does not work out in harmony with the practice. We have had some difficulty in regard to committees of this House. Committees of this House in charge of certain matters have undertaken to make recommendations in regard to money matters in some cases, while if the strict rule were enforced they could not do so ; yet, as they relate peculiarly to the constitution of the House, there is a disposition to overlook it. A little more latitude is given in regard to the Senate and the House of Commons than is allowed in any other department of the public service. Theoretically, the government has control over it, but practically, inasmuch as these affairs particularly affect the House of Commons and inasmuch as the House of Commons appoints a committee to deal with them, there is a reluctance on the part of the government to oppose the recommendation that it makes.
Who are the commissioners of internal economy in the Senate ?
They have no body of the same name. They have a committee.
They elect the committee themselves ?
Yes.
And the government appoint the commissioners of internal economy for this House ?
Yes.
And in the Senate ?
It is purely a committee in the Senate.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: In the Senate, does the committee act with the Speaker 1

Sometimes without him.
Mr. FOWLER, It depends upon the complexion of the House.
Then, it comes down to this, in so far as this House is concerned, that it is a question of the recommendation of the proper committee ?
Of the internal economy commissioners.
They are really members of the administration together with the Speaker ?

Yes.
The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COM-" MERGE. The Speaker is an ex-officio member.
Is there any committee of the House that has anything to do with the matter ?

No, except that there are committees in regard to printing and the ' Hansard.' These are the only committees that undertake to fix salaries and once in a while we have had to take exception to their recommendations.
at the close of the session I would endeavour to go to Moncton and take up a number of matters which would include that to which my attention had been drawn now. AVhile I was not able to give these gentlemen any definite assurance, I approached the matter sympathetically, because as respects some classes of workmen they were able to show that their wages are pretty low. Without committing myself, I assured them that I would look into the matter at the close of the session.
Is it not possible to do something this session ?
It can be dealt with through the general vote. It does not need any specific appropriation, because these gentlemen do not come under the Civil Service Act.
They take upon themselves to fix salaries ?
They have made recommendations to the House.

This House votes a certain amount of money for the contingencies of the Senate. This sum is placed at. the dispcsal of the committee and the Senate upon the recommendation of this committee fixes the salaries. That accounts for the fact that the salaries have been increased in the Senate this year and last year. It does seem very extraordinary that the doorkeeper of the House of Commons should receive $500 while the doorkeeper of the Senate receives double that amount. This case has been mentioned, but I understand that a disparity also exists in other cases as between the House of Commons and the Senate. Who should initiate the reform is something that I am not prepared to say at the moment. I thought perhaps it would complete the explanation to say, what has been done by the committee of the Senate when the amount is voted in the way I have stated.

There are some other deserving public servants in addition to the letter carriers, who will not be benefited by this Bill when it becomes law. I wish to ask the Minister of Finance, who is acting Minister of Railways, if many representations have not been made to him with regard to the remuneration paid to trackmen on the government railways, and if he proposes doing something in the matter ? These are very deserving public servants ; they are out in all weather ; they get very small remuneration, and if the minister would give an increase in the wage scale paid them, I believe it would be generally acceptable. I would like to ask him, if anything will be done to increase the wages of the trackmen ?
Some representations have recently been made to me on the subject. My time was very much occupied, but I assured the deputation that-

I move :
To amend section 18 by striking out the first, second and third lines down to the words ' sorters shall ' and inserting in lieu thereof the following :-
Section 10 of chapter 15 of -the statutes of 1895 and section 10 of chapter 14 of the statutes of 1900, are hereby repealed and the following is substituted the-refor :-
' T-he remuneration of messengers, porters, packers and sorters, temporary or permanent, and all temporary clerks and writers shall.'
In this amendment there Is a transposition of the words ' temporary or permanent ' or otherwise it might he held that the word ' temporary ' applied to all the classes.
What is the object to be attained by the amendment ?

The citation in the resolution was taken from the Civil Service Act, and is incorrect. In the resolution the word ' temporary ' being at the beginning, might make it appear that that word applied to each one of these classes. It is not intended to limit the provisions of the section to temporary messengers, but to apply it to messengers, port-ters, packers and sorters, but by putting that word at the beginning it would be applicable to them whether they be temporary or permanent. There is an old class of permanent messengers appointed in days gone by, but the more modern appointments are in the temporary class.

This would emphasize the suggestion of my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Birkett), that you should have a committee, or an investigation of some kind, so that some uniform system might prevail with regard to all employees of that kind. There is no particular reason why you should have some of them permanent and some temporary, except possibly in some cases. It would seem that as the necessities of the service have arisen, vacancies have been filled, rather by the appointment of temporary officers from time to time, than by any attempt to re-organize any particular department.
There has been a drift in that direction as regards the lower officers.
It seems to have resulted in a great deal of confusion. The more we discuss this measure, the more we realize that there is a great deal of wisdom in the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Birkett).

I do hope that before this Bill passes, the Postmaster General will announce to the House that he has adopted the suggestion of the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett), and that a committee will be appointed to inquire into the matter, and give equal justice to all classes.
It was mentioned to me, that in former years there were committees of the House appointed to investigate the workings of the different departments.

Not a committee of the House. A certain number of civil servants were appointed under the presidency of Mr. Courteney, Deputy Minister of Finance, and there is a voluminous report on the subject of grading and classifying.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: It was stated to me, that occasionally a committee of the House was appointed in former times to consider matters of this kind, and that was very much in line with the suggestion of my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Birkett).

If there is any committee appointed I hope it will result in more practical good, than the last civil service commission. That commission was appointed some few years ago, and it made a thorough Investigation and very voluminous report, but I think the fruits of their labour terminated with the making of the report. As to the suggestion of my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), that it was not yet too late to appoint a committee, I wish to express my regret that our predecessors left us so much housecleaning to do, that we only had time to take up the more pressing, matters, otherwise we would have been able to reach these other things that have been referred to. For instance, a great deal of the discussion to-day has been with regard to the restoration of third-class clerks, and if that class had not been abolished in 1895, we would not have to restore it now and we would not have had so much move time for dealing with these cases that have not yet been taken up.

While we are on the question of house-cleaning, I would point out to the Minister of Labour, that his government have been dirtying the house instead of cleaning it. There is no more vicious form of patronage than that perpetrated in the present resolution, with reference to the statutory increases. That sort of thing Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
tends to sap the independence of the whole service, and in a measure to destroy its usefulness by creating a lot of toadies when you make these men entirely subservient to the heads of departments. Of course it is to be hoped that there are men in the civil service with manhood enough to stand up against this, and I know there are hundreds of such men in the service, but at the same time the provision in this resolution puts a premium on subserviency and sycophancy, and tends to sap the independence of the civil service. There is no doubt about that.
I am sorry that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) has so expressed himself. The provisions in the resolution are in entire harmony with the principles applicable to all increases-
Not at all.

Increases under the Civil Service Act have always been determined by the government of the" day on the recommendation of the head of the department, and all that we do is to make the increase $50 instead of $30 in many cases, and to increase the maximum of several classes. All these increases will be made in entire harmony with the practice and the law as heretofore existing. In the name, and on behalf of the civil service of Canada, I regret that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) should say that the possibility of their getting increases will create a class of toadies and make them subservient, and sap their manhood. I have a higher opinion of civil servants than to believe that they so little value their manhood or their independence as to be influenced by a matter of that kind. My acquaintance with the civil servants leads me to believe, that there is nothing whatever to justify the suggestion of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) that they are not manly and independent enough to stand by their rights, even if doing so involves the loss of possible increases, or the favour or good-will of their ministers. They are a sterling and an independent class, so far as I know, and a manly class. I say that it is a gross injustice to them to state, that they so little value their manhood as to surrender it for the sake of the temporary, and comparatively trifling additions to their salaries, that are proposed to be made possible under this Bill.

The hon. gentleman has seized this opportunity to make a campaign speech. I made no insinuation against the civil servants of Canada, but I did say tliat the government had attempted to place the civil servants under their control, by making these increases dependent upon the favour of the heads of the departments. There is no question but that the civil servants of Canada will compare most favourably with any other class of our citizens, but vet, having some knowledge of nature, I have not the slightest doubt that there are some men among them, who, in

order to reap some present advantage, would be inclined to conceal tbeir real opinions. What I object to is, that this is an attempt on the part of the government to influence the civil servants. The Postmaster General says he is surprised that anybody should insinuate that men would be affected by this sort of thing. The Postmaster General himself would be one of the very first to bring that sort of pressure to bear in his own department. I have no doubt about that. It would not be the first time that the Postmaster General sinned in that direction. He would be the very first to compel men in his own department
Order.
I see you are shaking your head, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think it is in order to say that the hon. gentleman would be the first to bring improper influence to bear
Then I will not give him the chief position but I will say that he would be among the first, if that would make it more parliamentary.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not quite parliamentary yet.

I have read the opinions of colleagues of the Postmaster General, and their views are, that this principle of making increases of salaries attendant on ihe whim of the minister, is a bad principle. It may be that there is not a man in the civil service who would be affected by it. It may be that there is not a man in the civil service who would not forfeit $400 or $500 increase of salary, rather than act as a toady or sacrifice his independence in any way ? It is to be hoped that is so, but at the same time that does not justify legislation that would tend towards such a thing. I say that this legislation is vicious legislation, and should not be passed.

I am glad that the Postmaster General has acquiesced in the suggestion made by the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett), but the Postmaster General says that he has had so much housecleaning to do, that he has not had time to give to the consideration of this matter.
I repeat, that it is due to the efforts of the hon. member (Mr. Birkett), that this Bill is in as good shape as it is, and that the civil service are to get the relief contemplated by it. I would remind the Postmaster General that two years ago his leader said in the city of Toronto that he had nothing to reform. What has the Postmaster General done since that statement was made, to make any reform in the civil service ? What Acts have been passed since the present government came into power, to amend the Civil Service Act, except it be legislation which tended in the direction of giving more patronage to the ministers and des- *
troying the far better conditions which they found existing when they, came into office ? Surely the Postmaster General has not been doing any house-cleaning in the ordinary sense of the term ? And as to this Bill it. self, the Postmaster General has done more to obstruct its passage than any other man in this House. He occupied the whole forenoon in reading copious extracts from speeches made in 1S95, and most of which had no bearing on this discussion. No complaint as to that was made from this side of the House, because we are anxious to have fair legislation passed, and to make the Bill a just Bill. I am much obliged; however, to the Minister of Labour, for accepting the suggestion made by my esteemed friend and colleague (Mr. Birkett), and I trust that at next session of parliament we will have a proper Bill that will do justice to all' classes of the civil service.
Mr, REID (Grenville). I am much amused at the sympathetic nature of the Postmaster General for the civil service to-day. I would like to know if he ever increased the salary of a single official in his department without strong pressure having been brought to bear on him ? I firmly believe that no civil servant has ever got justice from him, without strong pressure being brought to bear from the outside. I do not think the hon. Postmaster General is different from the other ministers in that respect. I would like him to say if he ever increased one salary except under extreme pressure.

I have never interfered with the increases of the staff. My hon. friend is speaking entirely erroneously. The deputy of my department goes through the list and makes the recommendations. I have never dissented from his recommendations. I leave the matter of increases and promotions entirely in the hands of my deputy. He gathers information from those in [DOT] the service, and "makes to me! a report, which I act upon. The hon. gentleman' will not find any one in the Post Office Department to sustain him in the statement he has made. I trust that the staff of the department will read ' Hansard ' of this date. I call their attention to the attack made upon me as tbe head of the department, by the last speaker, and they who know how I have treated them will be the ones to deal with the hon. gentleman.

There is an end to almost everything, and we have very nearly reached the end of this resolution. Before we pass the last section, I wish to say that I fully appreciate what the hon. Postmaster General has done for the service. I feel grateful to him on the part of the service, particularly on the part of the lower paid class, that is, the temporary writers, messengers, porters, packers and sorters; but,



I am sorry that the hon. minister did not go further. A great many of these gentlemen are in his own department. I am sorry that he did not include the letter-carriers In this measure. We know that there is no more deserving class. In all kinds of weather they start out with their packs on their backs to serve everybody in the community. If there is one class who are deserving of more consideration than another, it is the letter-carriers. I hope that good will come out of this discussion in the future, and that the letter-carriers will not he forgotten.

With regard to the salaries of messengers, porters, packers and sorters, I can only inform the hon. gentleman-and I know that it will he grateful information to him-that when we took office the maximum salary which that most deserving class could reach was $500. In 1900 we increased the maximum by $100. This Bill increases it by $200, so that after this Bill passes the salary of a porter, a packer or a .sorter can go up to $700 as against the maximum of $500 under the previous administration. We have by this measure and the previons measure increased the salaries of these deserving officers 40 per cent. With regard to the salaries of the letter-carriers, under the law as it was left by our predecessors, they could only obtain a maximum of $000, and it took them nine years to reach that maximum, tinder the law as it is to-day, a letter-carrier can reach the maximum of $725 in about half the time. Thus there was an increase in the former case of 40 per cent and in the latter case of 20 per cent. I think these people are quite intelligent enough to understand the meaning of these increases, and they will not in the slightest .degree be deceived by the professed friendship of their professed friends on the opposite side of the House. Professions are one thing, practice is another. You gave them a stone we gave them bread.
Hard tack you are giving them.
I think it is time that we heard the last of our predecessors. They have not been in power since 1890. Let us forget our predecessors, and do what is Tight and just ourselves.

I made a very strong appeal the other evening on behalf of those who are getting very small salaries, such as $400 or $500 a year. I do not believe that these people are protected by this Bill as they should be, and I hope the Postmaster General will try and do something for them. The only minister whom I have found to be hardly fair in my constituency is the Postmaster General. We have officers of the customs and other departments there, but the only dismissal was by the Postmaster General, and I believe it was a most unfair one. The man only received

'
a small amount, and he was dependent upon it. The letter-carriers, as well as the other small-salaried officials should be considered. In framing this Bill, I think, the hon. minister has been hardly careful enough in protecting their rights.

My hon. friends seem to think we are not dealing fairly with those people who are getting $400 or $500 a year. I can only again make comparisons, which of course are odious ; but they are helpful in a discussion of this kind. The lowest paid class in the service in 1895 had a salary assigned to it of $400 at entrance, with increases of $30 a year till the maximum of $600 was attained, and it took nearly seven years for a man to attain that maximum. Under the measure now before the committee a temporary writer on appointment would get $500, an increase of 25 per cent to start with, which he carries through the whole time he is in the service ; and his annual increase, instead of being limited to $30, as under our predecessors, is made $50 under the present measure. So that he will now attain a maximum of $700 in four years. To that extent we are making a substantial betterment for that class, and I am satisfied that they will be able to discern it.

The hon. gentleman says that he is starting these men at $500 instead of 4H00 a year. Did not the hon. minister state on the floor of this House the other evening that the cost of living had increased 30 per cent in the last seven years 7
No, I made no statement.

Perhaps it was the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt). It was made from that side of the House. Does the hon. gentleman dispute the fact that the cost of living lias increased in the last seven years ?
Certainly not. It is the result of the good times.

Therefore a man who got $400 per annum formerly should now get $520 to make his position as good as it was when he was getting $400. You are giving him $20 per annum less than when he was getting $400 under the Conservative regime. Besides you have done away with superannuation. The hon. gentlemen must admit that these men are not in as good a position, even under the increase, as they were under the former government.

The hon. gentleman asks that the increase in the cost of living be made a measure of the increase in salary. That would involve a reduction in the proposed increases to a large class. For example, the porters and sorters, &c., whose salaries are now in-

creased to a maximum of $700, as against $500, are getting too much. The hon. gentleman says the increase in the cost of living is 30 per cent, but we have increased these salaries beyond 30 per cent, and according to the hon. gentleman's argument we should not increase them beyond the 30 per cent.
That is not my argument.
Did the hon. gentleman ever raise his voice when his party was in power in favour of doing justice to those officials ?
During the time the Conservatives were in power did the hon. gentleman ever stand up and advocate an increase ?
Often.

Why, the opposition did nothing but cry out against the extravagant pay given the civil servants. I am not arguing that the increase should be limited to 30 per cent, but I say that those who are receiving small salaries should be increased more in proportion than those receiving much higher salaries, because the latter can meet the increased cost of living much better than the former.
Let me make another comparison for the benefit of my hon. friend. Under the former regime, the annual increase to those employees was $30 per year, and now it is $50 a year, or 65 per cent more.

The hon. minister has not disposed of my argument that they are getting at least $20 per annum less, taking the increased cost of living into account, than they did under the former regime.
Mi-. CLARKE. This resolution was no doubt hurriedly prepared under the pressure put on the government by my hon. friend behind me (Mr. Birkett). But when the hon. minister makes a comparison, he should in all fairness admit that no provision was made for superannuation, and that these employees are not given as formerly, so many week's holidays ; and are deprived of other privileges.
They are not.

Men were better off eight or nine years ago than they are to-day, owing to the increased eost of living, if the advantages which were given in the way of superannuation be taken into account, it will be seen that they were better off under the old regime.

The Postmaster General has stated that if the Conservative government had remainded in power, the good times, which have increased the cost of 393i
living, would not have come about. I would ask him to point out what he has ever done to cause these good times ?
That would be a very long story.
Then give us an instalment at least.

I think my hon. friend from King's (Mr. Fowler) has hardly done justice to the Postmaster General. In the first place, the present government have increased the expenditure $3,000,000 or $4,000,000. That accounts for the good times. Then they have given us free trade as it is in England. That, no doubt, is responsible for our increased prosperity. Besides they have given the country prohibition, which no doubt has brought about increased revenue. Then they have amended the Acts regarding the independence of parliament, so that no longer can members of parliament be appointed to offices of emolument under the Crown. They have also absolutely destroyed protection, which was bleeding the farmers white. I am sorry that I have to come to the relief of the administration, but I could not see the hon. minister remain silent when an appeal of this kind was made to him, and therefore on his behalf, which is the only way I can act for the government, I have pointed out in what way this government has brouht about the good times.

My hon. friend the leader of the opposition has omitted one circumstance. He has omitted to mention the benefit which this country has derived from the fact that he separated himself from the Liberal party to become the leader of the opposition, and in this way enabled the government to retain office and put its policy into practicable operations. My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has had sufficient regard for the public interest to change his views on the question. I congratulate the country that the views he now enunciates, since he ceased to be a member of the Liberal party, have little chance of going on the statute-book of Canada.	*

My hon. friend the Postmaster General in a somewhat clumsy attempt to answer my argument has not done himself justice. Does he not know that sitting along side of him, immediately on his left, is a gentleman who for year's was a valued member of the Conservative party and who for some years past has been an equally valued member of the Liberal party.
' The POSTMASTER GENERAL. That shows his good judgment.
ail'. BORDEN (Halifax). Perhaps I might claim an equally good judgment in view" of the circumstances under which I was led to withdraw my allegiance from the Liberal party of which he is so proud. There are

some other members of the present administration of whom the same thing may be said. But we are not dealing with the question of a change of party allegiance; we are dealing with the question of a change of policy and principles within that same party. My hon. friend the Postmaster General was good enough to introduce this subject of the good times
They are everywhere.

So I suppose there is no harm in discussing it in general. I shall endeavour, on behalf of the Postmaster General as he did not seem able to do it himself, to point out a few of the reasons to which we may ascribe the good times we have had in the country in the past two years. Does the Postmaster General deny that these good times have been very largely due to-the fact that we have at present free trade as it is in England. He knows that is the policy of his party to which the Prime Minister has pledged himself over and over again on public platforms in this country and to which I have no doubt my hon. friend himself is pledged. Are not the good times owing to the fact that this has- become an 'accomplished fact) jitn this country ? It must have become an accomplished fact otherwise my hon. friend the Postmaster General would certainly protest. And is it not also due to the fact that we have destroyed protection ? The Minister of Trade and Commerce knows how he characterized that alleged evil influence over the fortunes of Canada in days gone by and I am sure the Minister of Trade and Commerce would be the first to stand up and establish to the satisfaction of himself, if to the satisfaction of no one else, that protection is absolutely a thing of the past in Canada. I forgot to refer a moment ago to the granting of bonuses to different industries in this country. This is something against which my hon. friends on the other side absolutely protested in days gone by. Is it not true that the good times we have at present are largely due to the fact that that policy has been largely done away with by the government ?
I am very curious to know under what section of the legislation with which we are now dealing my hon. friend is speaking.

I am speaking on exactly the same clause of the resolution as that upon which my hon. friend the Postmaster General was speaking when he first made this utterance. I hope I have satisfied my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The discussion for the last few minutes has been wholly out of order, taking a wide range on what caused the good times in Canada. The matter now under discussion is clause IS of the resolution and the discussion must be confined to that clause.

Is it the intention of the government to increase the pay of the sessional messengers, either by way of bonus or in any other way ? They have been doing very onerous duties here for the last six months, and I would ask if it is the intention of the government to recognize their faithful service ?
This Bill enumerates certain classes to which it applies; if they are within these classes the measure will apply to them; if they are not it will not apply to them.
The section refers to messengers, packers, temporary clerks, &c.
I have answered my hon. friend, have I not ?
I do not understand so. The officers to whom I referred are those connected with the House here, messengers, writers, &e.

I have mentioned at an earlier stage of this discussion that all officers and employees of the House of Commons and Senate are dealt with by those bodies. They are not officers appointed by the government and do not come under the provisions of the Civil Service Act.

I desire to ask the Postmaster General an important question. He lias stated that those of the civil servants who come under this Act will be very much better off than under former governments, that they will now get their statutory increase of $50 a year in addition to an increase of twenty-five per cent in salary. I want to ask the Postmaster General if he intends to keep faith with these persons who are getting the statutory increases any better than he kept it with those whom he found entitled to statutory increases when he came into office, and as a general all round evidence of recantation on his part, if he will restore the statutory increases that were withheld during the period he has been in office ?
The POSTMASTER GENERAL The Bill does not meet the case to wrhich my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) refers; it provides for two new classes and also increases the maximum and minimum salaries in certain other classes and increases the annual amount that may be awarded to those who are in these classes. Such, I think, is fairly the scope of the Bill. My hon. friend is so intelligent and astute that I am sure I would only offend his dignity if I attempted to illuminate him on any matter which is so plainly set forth on the face of the measure.

I did not ask the hon. gentleman what the scope of the Bill was, I asked the hon. gentleman if he intended to keep faith in a matter that is not in the Bill. This BUI will make it no more binding upon the hon. gentleman to pay statu-

tory increases than the law that he found when he came into office. I would like to know whether the hon. gentleman intends to keep faith and to pay the statutory increases ? I think I heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce state that it was optional on the part of the heads of the departments to pay these statutory increases.
I hardly think my hon. friend expects an answer to that question. Those who are in the service of the government of Canada require no guarantee that it will keep faith with them.

I would like to ask the Postmaster General one question. There was a gentleman appointed some years ago as assistant clerk of the House at a salary of $2,800 ; in 1S97 he was dismissed and the government has been giving him $840 a year ever since. When he was dismissed the government appointed Mr. Laplante as assistant clerk, at a salary of only $2,000 a year. Now is it right to give Mr. Laplante only $2,000 a year for performing the services for which Mr. Rouleau received $2,800 a year, and is now getting $840 a year since he resigned ? I have heard a good deal about the increase of salaries, but there should be no decrease.

I can only explain to my hon. friend, as I have had occasion to explain to others earlier in the discussion, that the salaries of the officials of the House are not fixed by the government, but the Internal Economy Committee. It would be regarded as an interference with the privileges of parliament for the government to assume to take control of the appointments, dismissals and salaries of the officials of this House. Their salaries are substantially under control of the House of Commons. If any official thinks he is not being properly remunerated, there is the Committee on Internal Economy to whom he can apply, and who will deal with the matter.
On clause 19,
' 19. All sums of money voted by parliament for the financial year ending on the 30th day of June, 1904, for the payment of the salaries or the increases to the salaries of any persons now in the public service, shall, in the event of the promotion of any such persons to higher classes or grades, or on Ithetir transfer t* other positions in the public service, be applicable in or towards payment of the salaries or increases to the salaries of such persons so promoted or transferred, and during the financial year ending on the 30th day of June, 1904, there may be paid from and out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada such sums of money as may not have been voted by parliament, but which may be required for payment of such [DOT]salaries and increases of salaries as are authorized by this Act.

I propose to amend that by inserting after the words ' public service,' the following words :
Or their becoming entitled to or being granted increases of salary under the provisions of this Act.	.
And after the word ' transferred,' to insert the words :
Or becoming entitled to or being granted increases an aforesaid.
I will explain these two changes. The clause provides for the payment of increases, and it has been pointed out that unless it is amended where we have increased the maximum of a class say from $1,000 to $1,100, a man still remains in that class, and is not eligible for an increase. These words are simply to cover a case of that kind.
Is not the last part of that rather unusual-a provision that, money can be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund without being voted by parliament ?

Specifically it is unusual. But it is only for the fraction of a year, and it will involve a good deal of tedious work iu making up the accounts, there are so many officers that it will apply to, and this is to simplify the procedure.

I suppose we will simplify it if we do away altogether with the voting of estimates by parliament. But it would not be a simplicity desirable in the public interest. I think the Postmaster General ought to give us some information as to what the sums of money will he, what amounts will be required, to what purposes they will he devoted. If we are to pass over the estimates we ought to have some information that would justify us.

My hon. friend's objection is not unreasonable. But if this resolution goes though committee, before the Bill is read a third time, or iu supply, I will endeavour to get the figures and furnish them. It will only be possible at present to go through the whole service and make out a list of all the possible increases, but it would not be possible for each department to prepare them for the supplementary estimates. If the moneys had to be voted by the supplementary estimates, it would be necessary for each department to go through the whole question of increases and promotions, and the promotions would have to be settled, which is always a time-killing affair. If there are between one andi two thousand of that class in the city of Ottawa, it would hardly be possible for the deputy heads to prepare their recommendations in time for the supplementary estimates.

This is really an appropriation by parliament. This resolution is as much an appropriation by parliament as an estimate would be, so that there is really no evasion of the rule whatever. We vote money by estimates and we

vote money by resolutions as much as by estimates, so that this specially conforms to the rule that parliament must vote the money.
You might say that parliament was voting the money if it voted iu one lump sum $50,000,000 for the government.
We are not voting it in a lump sum. We are voting it in detail.

I do not see any detail here. The resolution simply says that:
During the financial year ending the 30th day of June, 1904, there may be paid from and out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund *f Canada such sums of money as may not have been voted by parliament, but which may be required for payment of such salaries and increases of salaries as are authorized by this Act.
It amounts practically to this that you have in this resolution and in the Bill which will be founded upon it, a provision that the Governor in Council can in his discretion make certain increases in salaries. Then, you have the provision that whatever increases the Governor in Council may make in that way shall be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund. It is a very different thing from voting the money by estimate. Here there is no opportunity for inquiry, there is no detail, and there Is not the information that is usually given to the House in regard to matters of that kind. That is the objection I have to it. I would doubt very much whether there is any precedent for it.
This is only for a portion of one year.

I do not wish to stand in the way of deserving gentlemen receiving the increases in salary to which [DOT] they may be entitled, but at the same time, I do not wish to be understood as assenting to a departure from the proper parliamentary rules.

The vote for the civil service has already been placed before parliament, and a general and detailed discussion has taken place in regard to it. This is to provide for the difference between the amount voted, upon which all proper information has been given, and the sum authorized by these resolutions to be paid. I cannot see the difference between doing it in this way and doing it by way of supplementary estimates. If we were to bring* down supplementary estimates saying that there shall be so many thousand dollars applied for the purpose of doing what we now propose to do, they would not give any more information than is afforded by these resolutions.

It is certainly a departure from the regular form of procedure. Although in itself the thing may not be ab-Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
solutely harmful, yet, as affording a precedent for a departure from the general procedure, it may be very harmful. I have not yet seen any very great necessity for it. I do not see why the resolution cannot be brought down in the form of a supplementary estimate, when there will be an opportunity of discussing the matter in detail. This is a matter of very great importance, and it involves a very distinct departure from the regular and proper procedure.

I do not see that there is any departure from the regular and proper procedure whether we bring down a document that we call estimates or bring down' a document that we call resolutions. It amounts to the same thing in both cases. I cannot see that if we were to bring down a supplementary estimate that we would give hon. gentlemen opposite any further information than we have in this resolution, unless we took every individual in the service and put down the additional amount he is to get. That would give a very elaborate statistical statement without adding anything to our information. It would be simply authorizing the Governor in Council to give these increases, and as we know from what has taken place in the House before, what the salaries of the different parties amount to, we know too in regard to this resolution that it authorizes the Governor in Council to pay the higher salaries rather than the lower salaries which have already been passed in the form of estimates in this House.

But this is a departure from the general procedure because we are voting an amount which is not specifically stated. The thing is entirely indefinite. It says that an amount which has not been voted by parliament shall be paid.

But my hon. friend will see that it is not indefinite, that it is limited in every case by restrictions which this Act applies. You can vote in any given case to increase the salary of any given official and limit it just as the Act says it shall be limited. This is not a departure from sound principle at all.
It is a departure because the principle is that you must bring in estimates.
This is an estimate.	*

This is not an estimate in which the sum is definitely stated as it should be in an estimate. In itself it may not be very harmful, but it may form a precedent for something that will be harmful, and it certainly is a violation of the custom and procedure of the House, which requires that an estimate shall always be prepared and a certain fixed amount placed in the estimate and then that information shall be given to the House as to how that money is to be expended. In this case you

simply say tliat this money shall be paid out without the vote of parliament.

Not
without the vote of parliament. It is a vote. We are now voting the money.

It says :
There may be .paid from and out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada such sums of money as may not have been voted by parliament.
' Already voted ' would have been better. But, this is a vote.

It is not, and the language of the resolution itself justified the statement I made.
There may be paid from and oyt of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada such sums of money as may not have been voted by parliament. but which may be required for payment of such salaries and increases of salaries as are authorized !by this Act.
Of course that does, in a certain sense, I admit, limit the amount of money paid out. However, the hon. Minister of Finance must agree with me that this is a departure from the usual procedure in voting money, and I question very much whether a precedent can be found for voting money Without defining the amount. ' Why is it necessary to make this departure ? Surely you could bring down a supplementary estimate. The supplementaries are not down yet.

I think there will be no trouble in forming a rough estimate of what the amount is that will be required. I do not agree, however, with my hon. friend that there is anj' departure from the ordinary procedure. My hon. friend is mistaken when he says that parliament always states exactly the sum that it votes. There are cases in which it does not. There are sometimes votes in which you cannot specify the exact amount. Take for instance, the case of the bounties on iron and steel. You fix the amount per ton, but you can pay for as many tons as are produced.
In the estimates this year you put a certain amount down for bounties, did you not ?
No.
You did not fix the amount ?

No.
Mr. FOWLER, What did you pay that out of ?

We paid it out of the consolidated revenue fund. There is a permanent statute. Whether you bring down a resolution and crystallize it into a statute or whether you bring down an estimate and crystallize it into another form of statute the rule is the same. In both cases the money is voted.
Mr. FOWLER, It seems to me that it would be better if you could make an estimate.

I have no doubt that before the matter is through my hon. friend can give an estimate as to what amount this will probably involve. The limitation is in the amount which we are authorized to pay to each individual official.
I admit that to a certain extent, but at the same time it is a departure from the usual custom.

I will endeavour to gather the information so that it can be announced in Committee of Supply.
Mr. FOWLER, You can state the amount when the Bill is brought down.
It is hardly worth while keeping the Bill back for that.

I wish to ask the acting Minister of Railways, if the government intends to increase the pay of the trackmen on the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railways. I am informed that these employees are not paid nearly as good wages as are the employees on other railway systems in the Dominion. If that is so, such an injustice should be remedied at once. I have had several communications with reference to this matter, I beg to read the following resolution from Arden, Manitoba, which will explain itself :
Moved by Brother Woolsey, seconded by Brother J. Wilson : That we, the members of Minnedosa Division No. 163, of Maintenance ot Way Employees of America assembled, do by unanimous vote desire to place on record, that we strongly disapprove of the low scale of wages paid by the government roads of Canada to the maintenance of way employees, such wages being below the wages paid by other Canadian roads for same class of labour, and we wish as voters to enlist your aid, both in the House and out of it, towards rectifying this injustice. Carried.
Yours truly,
Signed on behalf of the lodge,
JOHN MUIRHEAD, President, W. J. DUNCAN, Secretary.
If we are going to increase the pay of nearly all the civil servants in the employ of the government, is there any reason why the trackmen on the government railways should be singled out for exceptional treatment ? The cost of their living has iucreased in the same proportion as the cost of living to other civil servants, and they should get an increase in pay as well as the others.

The hon. gentleman was not in the House this afternoon when a similar question was asked, and I answered with regard to the trackmen on the Intercolonial Railway As to the Prince Edward Island Railway, some increase in the wages of some of the trackmen has recently been made. I may say, how-

ever, that the whole matter is under consideration.

I wish to add my voice, in favour of an increase of wages being given to the employees on the government railways. While I am not opposed to increasing the salaries of the civil servants of Ottawa, yet, at the same time, when we talk about men getting a minimum salary of $500 a year for working six or seven hours a day, we should remember that on the Intercolonial Railway there are men working ten hours a day
And sometimes fifteen hours a day.

Yes, and sometimes fifteen hours a day; and yet these hardworking employees have to be content with a salary of slightly over $400 a year. For a number of years past I have given considerable attention to this question. I know that the reply is usually given that the wages paid to the trackmen on the Intercolonial are relatively as high as the wages paid on other roads. In my opinion that is no argument. On a government railway we should pay a man what he is worth, irrespective of what private corporations may pay their employees. I do trust that when the acting Minister of Railways goes down to Moncton, as he has promised, and meets the representatives of the trackmen, he will take this matter into his most serious consideration. I hope he will not make two bites at a cherry, but that he will give these men a good living wage. The hon. minister will find when he meets the trackmen, that they are a reasonable lot of men, and that they desire nothing but what is honestly their due. They are devoted to the service of the Intercolonial Railway. We boast of the splendid road-bed and the equipment of that railway, but we should not forget that the men who keep that track in first-class order are not paid a fair remuneration for their arduous labour. I believe it has been suggested by the trackmen themselves, that there should be a difference in the wages paid to men living in country districts, and to those living in incorporated towns where rents are higher and living expenses are greater. That, however, is a matter of detail. Speaking for the Intercolonial Railway trackmen of Cumberland county, I may say that they appreciate what this government has already done for them, it is only a few years since they were working for a few cents over a dollar a day.
For ninety-nine cents.
My hon. friend from Westmoreland says that some years ago they only received ninety-mine cents a day.
When was that ?
Under the Conservative administration.
It is a very long time ago since they got any such pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: When this government came into power, if I remember right, the trackmen were paid only $1.10 a day.

One dollar and fifteen
cents.

At present they are paid $1.30. These trackmen are not agitators; they are grateful for what the government has done for them in the past, and the minister will find them to be an intelligent and hard working body of men. Surely they should be paid by the government at least $1.50 a day ? No man in any part of Canada can maintain a family at a less wage than that. I am glad, Sir, that this question has been so favourably received on both sides of the House. There should be no politics in a question of this kind. These trackmen are amongst the most deserving of our public employees. They give the best of their brawn and sinew to the service of the country, and when they get old they have to retire without superannuation or pension of any kind. There is no class of the servants of the government, who are more worthy of every consideration.

I am glad that the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) has thought fit to say a word for the trackmen on the Intercolonial Railway, after having been urged twice from this side of the House

*
Will my hon. friend allow me ?
He comes from a section where there are a large number of railway employees
I am much obliged to you for refusing to let me say a word in explanation.

I would suggest that the Minister of Labour should take some little time to look into the grievances of the poor workingmen on the Intercolonial Railway whom the member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) has depicted as being so badly treated by the government. I trust that the trackmen on the government railways will receive a fair day's wage for a fair day's work.

I regret that my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) would not allow me to make an explanation; a courtesy which almost any gentleman of this House would extend to another. However, that is his own affair. I may mention that when the matter was first brought up a few minutes ago, I was in the whip's room, and when I returned to the chamber I took the first opportunity of calling the attention of the government to the grievances of the trackmen. I repeat once more that I have no desire to make political capital out of such a serious situation; but I can tell my hon. friend from Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) that long before he was in this House I spoke on the matter; I

went to the ministers in private about it; I introduced delegates to the minister, I waited on Mr. Pottinger and other officials of the Intercolonial, and I have been tireless in my efforts to better the condition of these men. They have already got an increase of pay, but I contend#that their present wage is altogether too low to enable them to maintain themselves and their families.

Surely, Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) has made a reference to this matter-

speechtext: Well, it is just this way : Sometimes an irrelevant debate is thrust upon us, and it appears to me that it is going too far.

In reference to what the hon. member for Cumberland has said about introducing politics into this matter of the trackmen on the Intercolonial Railway, I think the hon. gentleman himself was the first to introduce politics. Why was it necessary for him in making his plea on behalf of these men, to cast reflections on What the previous government did ?
I was asked when these men were paid the low sum of ninety-nine cents a day. [DOT]

The hon. gentleman was told by the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson), and he stated that the former government had paid them ninety-nine cents. I quite agree that these men should have larger pay, because their present pay is altogether insufficient for the service they perform, particularly when compared with what is paid on other roads. Much larger wages are paid on the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway and other roads than are paid to the trackmen along the line of the Intercolonial Railway. I think the rate of wages should be set by the government rather than by outside corporations.
Did the hon. gentleman state that the wages paid to the maintenance of way men on the Grand Trunk are greater than those paid on the Intercolonial V	>
I may be wrong about the Grand Trunk, but I aiii entirely right about the Canadian Pacific Railway.

the hon. member sit down ? When an hon. member is called to order, according to rule 12 he has to sit down. No hon. member has a right to lecture the presiding officer. If he disagrees with his decision, he can either appeal to the House or refer the matter to tlie Speaker.
He can discuss it.
