speechtext: If a member wishes to discuss a point of order, he can do so ; but he cannot stand in his place and lecture the chairman.
Then the chairman will admit that he was in error in putting the question before there was a discussion on it. If he will allow that, we will go on.

That was the only reference I made to the chairman. I have the

most profound respect, not only for tlie Chair,' but for the hon. gentleman himself.
Order.
I do not know how I am out of order.
Sarcastic.

I am not sarcastic. 1 say 1 hare the most profound respect both for the Chair and its occupant. He was putting the question before I had a chance to speak, and I said that as he was such a stickler for the rules, I would have to be too. With respect to what the hon. member for Cumberland brought forward as to the pay of the trackmen, I consider the demand of the men for $1.50 per day, a very moderate one, indeed, and I trust that this committee will deal with them fairly. I hope the Minister of Labour will not be on that commission, because he has such an inferior idea of what labour is worth in this country that he will certainly try to keep the wages down. But I think the Minister of Finance will take a different view ; I think he will be inclined to deal fairly with the men. I have that opinion of the Minister of Finance, and I trust that that opinion will be justified when he meets them. It seems to me that the government should pay all classes of men who serve the country ample remuneration for their services, from the highest rung of the ladder down to the lowest. In that way the government would set an example to other employers of labour. Labour would be more apt to receive its fair reward. When the corporations can point to men in the government service who are getting only $1.30 per day, it seems a good answer to give to those who are asking them for a fair wage. I do not see how a man can exist and bring up a family on less than $1.50 a day. It seems a very small amount, and when these men are asking for only that small advance, I think the government would be derelict in their duty if they refused to grant it. There should be a shaking up all round with respect to wages, because, as has been pointed out over and over again, the cost of living has very largely increased throughout the whole world, and it is only fair that the increase of wages should at least keep pace with the increased cost of living. Not only have the prices of things we use largely gone up, but we are living in a more luxurious age than we did ten or fifteen or twenty years ago, and it is only fair that the man who works with his hands should have some share in the luxuries. He requires more than the mere means to exist. He should be able to clothe his family decently, and to educate his children so that the child of the poorest man will have an equal chance with the child of the richest man to rise to the highest position in the land, even the exalted position of a member of the parliament of Canada. I trust that the government will take this matter into their serious considera-Mr. FOWLER.
tion, leaving politics aside, and looking at it with a desire to get at the bottom facts, and to ascertain just what amount is a fair remuneration for the services performed. I trust that they will make it a wholesale matter, applicable to the whole service outside as well as inside.#
I hope that the Postmaster General will revise his opinion regarding how the officials in his department are paid. I hope that the postmasters will receive that increase to which they are entitled. In our small towns our postmasters receive from $1,000 to $1,200 and are obliged to employ a clerk, so that they are really paid only what would be given an ordinary clerk. Men who hold a responsible office of that kind should receive more pay than the maximum of a third class clerk. They are a class to which the hon. gentleman should give his attention and whose remuneration he should largely increase. Take the letter-carriers for whom the hon. gentleman seems to have a special dislike. He does not seem willing to grant them any measure of justice, although he knows they have to be out in all sorts of weather and at all times of the day and their work is very severe. Hitherto they have not received that consideration to which they are entitled. These resolutions afford a certain measure of relief, which will affect about 20 per cent of the civil service, but they should be made wider. Their scope should be extended so as to embrace both the inside and outside service. I trust that in view of the representations from both sides of the House, in view of what the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) has strongly urged respecting the Intercolonial and of the representations of the senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Bel-court) and others, the government will consider the whole matter. What was done twenty years ago should not be allowed any weight.' The government were supposed to administer our affairs to suit the altered circumstances.
Growing times.

Certainly, but I hope the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) does not intend to imply that this government has done anything towards assisting the growing times. If he does I shall be glad to know what it Is. Perhaps be will take up the challenge, which I threw down to the Postmaster General.
Six o'clock.
If the hon. gentleman dees not wish the Bill to pass before six o'clock we may as well take recess.

The hon. minister has been obstructing the Bill himself. Surely he does not expect us to remain silent while he casts insinuations upon the Conservatives and the late government. If he wants to get this Bill through he should hold himself and his followers in hand.

I wish to ask whether the Auditor General is affected by this Bill and whether in the case where an appointment is made to grade A the promotion of a first-class clerk to grade A creates a vacancy owing to the fact that a first-class clerk of a department is promoted to grade A.

The hon. gentleman will observe that section 1 provides that the salary of a deputy head of a department on appointment shall be $3,500 with an annual increase up to $4,000. Then there are three special cases to which that limitation does not apply. On referring to the civil service list I see that the Auditor General is already at that maximum of $4,000.
It will not affect him.
No, because he is already at the maximum rate. I do not know whether that is by an Act of parliament.
It is by a special Act.

He is, of course, not dismissable by the government. In answer to that second question of the hon. gentleman it will be observed on reference to thei resolution that the promotion to grade A must be from a chief clerkship, not from a first-class clerkship. Grade A is an advance on the chief clerkship and Is treated as a clerkship of an additional class and therefore if the chief clerk were promoted to the rank of grade A that would leave a vacancy.
It would create a vacancy although perhaps that vacancy would not always be filled.
If a chief clerk was promoted into grade A there would be no chief clerk.

You might not want one. Supposing you had an officer who was especially deserving of promotion and you (promoted him to grade A but did not in any way alter his duties. In a case of that kind, although a vacancy would be technically created, it would not be necessary to appoint an extra clerk.

My hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) wanted to know whether grade A is a distinct class. The resolution provides :
In addition to the class of chief clerkships referred to in sections 15 and 16 of the said Act, another class to be known as ' Chief Clerkship, grade A ' is hereby created.
I think my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) will consent now to withdraw his
motion, which, if carried, would destroy the Bill.
I simply wished to test whether the minister was actually in earnest in his desire to push the Bill through, and would call in his majority to vote my motion down.

My hon. friend is not going to press his motion so I presume it is to be withdrawn.
Mr.' HUGHES (Victoria). If it be the pleasure of the committee I shall withdraw it.
Motion (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) withdrawn.

The hon. Minister of Finance suggested that in the third line from the bottom of clause 19 the word ' already ' be inserted. It may not be necessary but it can do no harm and the line will then read :
Such sums of money as may not already have been voted.
Section as amended agreed to.
The POSTMASTER GENERAL moved the reconsideration of sections 1, 2 and 3 and of subsection 2, of clause 4.
Motion agreed to.

The point is that these sections deal with the deputy heads and my attention has been called to the fact that there are two officers in the service who are deputies by Act of parliament, who have the rank of deputy head and are entitled to be included and it is thought that the Auditor General might be of opinion that they are not deputy heads within the meaning of this clause. The two officers in question are the Comptroller of the Mounted Police, Col. White, and Dr. Dawson, of the Printing Bureau. They have the status of deputy heads and are therefore entitled to come in under this provision. To prevent any doubt on the subject I propose to insert after the word ' department ' in the first line the words :
Or an officer having by statute the rank of a deputy head.	[DOT]
Similar words will be placed within the succeeding clause.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 2,

I wish to move that in clause 2 the same change be made ; that after the word ' heads ' in that second line the words ' and persons ' be added. That is after the word ' head ' where it secondly appears in that line so that it will read :
For the purpose of determining the salary of such deputy heads and persons, &c.
Section, as amended, agreed to.

On section 3,

I move to similarly amend the third section by inserting after the word ' head ' :
Or such other person having by statute the rank of a deputy head.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
With reference to subsection 2 of section 4, I move to add the words ' per annum ' after the word ' dollars ' in the second line, and also after the word ' dollars ' in the fourth line.

Before we pass that section I want to suggest to the Postmaster General a change, which I think on explanation he will readily accept. You will notice that the salary of a chief clerk, grade A, is fixed by the Act to run from a minimum of $2,400 to a maximum of $2,800. The salary of a chief clerk of the other grade, we will call it grade B, is $1,900 for the minimum and $2,500 for the maximum. It will be noticed that there is an overlapping. For instance, a chief clerk it may be, is receiving a sum of $2,500, and it may be desired to promote him into grade A, the minimum salary of which is $2,400 ; according to the resolution he would, unless some provision is made to the contrary, be appointed at the minimum of that class $2,400. So you have, if I may use the expression, an Irish promotion so far as the salary is concerned. I would suggest that if a chief clerk is promoted to grade A he should be promoted at the minimum of grade A as fixed by these resolutions, namely at $2,500.
You mean the maximum ?

No, the minimum of grade A is $2,500 and the maximum $2,S00. The minimum of a chief clerk is $1,900 and the maximum $2,500 ; so the maximum of a chief clerk is $100 higher than the minimum of grade A. So if you wish to promote a chief clerk to grade A you would have to appoint him at a salary of $100 less than he had been receiving previously. I would suggest to the Postmaster General that he put some words in the Bill to cover that case.	*
I think the idea would be carried out by providing that he should be promoted to the chief clerk A at a maximum salary of grade B.

To relieve my hon. friend of any anxiety on the subject-he called my attention to this matter some days ago-I would remind him that this resolution deals only with the money part, the voting of the money. I have a Bill founded upon this resolution in which there are provisions that are not contained in the resolution, because the resolution only contains such matters as refers to the voting of money. The Bill will contain this clause,

which I think will meet the case pointed out by my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt).
If a person on appointment ito a chief clerkship grade A is -at the time of such appointment in T&cedpt of a salary greater than the minimum salary of such chief clerkship as above provided, he may be appointed to such chief clerkship at thie salary he is then in receipt of, provided it does not exceed the maximum salary of such chief clerkship as above provided.
He carries his salary into the new class.
That is all right.
I think there are other cases of the same kind. For instance, I think you will find that the junior second class clerks afford cases of overlapping.
That is the only case I think.
The maximum of one is the minimum of the other.

I think the provision in the Bill covers the case. There is another provision which I would like to see the minister adopt, that is with reference to the case of the gentlemen who have been recently appointed to a class. For instance, a gentleman, I will say, has recently been appointed to the first class, the minimum salary of which under the old Act was $1,400. By these resolutions the minimum salary of a first-class clerk is going to be $1,500. It is a question with me whether, on the passing of this Bill, that clerk, who is now a first-class clerk only receiving $1,400, will be entitled to receive the increase of $100 which is added to the minimum of that class. Now, it is possible that the provision which says that the minimum salary of a first-class clerk should be $1,500 per annum, with an annual increase of $50 to a maximum of $1,900 per annum, is sufficient. It may be that a gentleman who has been recently appointed to the first class at $1,400 may be able to get the $1,500 under the Act, but there is some doubt about it, and I would invite the Postmaster General to make it clear in his Bill.
Amendments agreed to, and subsection, as amended, agreed to.

I have another suggestion to make to the Postmaster General which I hope he will deem worthy of consideration. I would suggest that the Bill be made to go into force on the 1st of July, 1903, in order to enable the clerks to get the advantage for the present year of the increases which are provided for in the Act. By applying the provisions of the resolution to the different people who are to-day in the civil service it becomes apparent that quite a number are not going to receive any benefit from the increase of salaries provided for in the different classes for per-

haps two, three, four or five years. It will take a clerk receiving a salary of $700 a year six years before he gets up to $1,000. By receiving an increase of $50 a year one can see at once that a clerk will only get the full benefit of this increase after the lapse of six years. That is so in other cases, though in a smaller degree. Some will reach the maximum in five and a half years, some in four years, and so on. My suggestion to the Postmaster General is that a provision be inserted in the Bill that the Bill shall come into force on the 1st July, 1903. Then, coupled with that suggestion, I have another which I can only make as a suggestion, and which I cannot offer by way of amendment or in any other way. Hon. gentlemen will remember that when I advocated an increase of salary to the civil service, I advocated it all around, I advocated that everybody employed in the government should receive consideration, and the basis upon which I urged that was that there had been a large increase in the cost of living. It must be apparent that if there has been an increase in the cost of living for those who receive the higher salaries there has also been an increase in the cost of living for those receiving smaller salaries, and one cannot help but remember that salaries ought to be increased all around. I am very grateful on behalf of the civil service for what has been done, but it is apparent that some 'members of the civil service are not going to get any immediate benefit from the Act, and as they are in need of some immediate relief, I now suggest that not only shall the Act be made to come into force on the 1st July, 1903, but that this year a provision be put in the estimates to allow of the giving of a bonus of $50 all around. I think that if we were to make it $100. possibly I would not be- asking too much, but I hope the suggestion will commend itself to the executive that a bonus of $50 be granted to the civil service. This is not a new proposal; there are precedents for it, and there are precedents which ought to be of considerable weight with a Liberal government, because, as I have had occasion to point out, in 1S74 a bonus of $75,000 was voted by parliament and paid to the civil servants. It was voted again in 1875, and I am informed that in 1S76 a bonus of $30,000 was voted in favour of the civil service. Hon. gentlemen who have taken part in this discussion have admitted the fact which cannot successfully be controverted that the cost of living has been very largely increased within the last few years. I think the country would be quite prepared to justify the executive if, iu order to relieve the stringency which unquestionably exists among a certain class of the civil servants, they were to grant them immediate compensation in the shape that I have suggested. I make the suggestion hoping that it will receive the earnest consideration of the executive and that they will make provision this year for the payment of $50 all around so that everybody in the civil service may be able to receive some benefit out of this resolution. There are quite a number who are not going to get any relief from this Bill for two, three, four or perhaps five years. I think the country would justify a measure of that kind, and 1 commend it to the earnest consideration of the executive.

Nothing would give me more pleasure than to support a resolution, or Bill, or anything else the government bring in for the purpose of carrying out the suggestion of the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt). I certainly think, that, in view of the fact that so many members of the civil service have been deprived of statutory increases to which they were entitled, we should go a little farther and make it $100 all around if it is possible.
, Make it $200.

I would make it $300. But, this is too serious a matter to joke about. I think this is a matter that should have been attended to long ago, and I would be only too pleased if the government would take it into consideration and act upon the suggestion. I am satisfied that as far as this side of the House is concerned, it will get no opposition. As far as the suggestion of the hon. gentleman goes in respect to making this measure retroactive in its effect, I think that is already provided for by clause 19, which says :
In the event of the promotion of any such persons to higher classes or grades, or on their transfer to other positions in the public service, he applicable in or towards payment of the salaries or increases to the salaries of such persons so promoted or transferred, and during the financial year ending on the 30th day cf June, 1904, there may be paid from and out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada such sums of money as may not have been voted by parliament, but which may be required for payment of such salaries and increases of salaries as are authorized by this Act.
If it is not intended I would ask the hon. Postmaster General to have whatever increases the civil servants are entitled to receive made payable from the 1st of July, 1903.

I may be permitted to inform the committee that there is a branch of the service here belonging to the outside service, the statistical branch, in connection with the Customs Department. The officers engaged in this service were brought here abou* two years ago. They were gathered from the different custom houses throughout the country, and while they are obliged to remain in Ottawa they do not have the advantages of those who are in the inside service. I would ask the hon. Postmaster General if provision is made for these members of the service ? I know that there are quite a number from

the eastern provinces, that there are quite a number from the western provinces and that they are to all intents and purposes members of the inside service, but that they do not have the advantages of the emoluments which belong to that service. A great many of them came here receiving very small salaries and they have not been increased. I would ask if provision is made for remedying the grievances which they have.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I fully agree with what has been said by the hon. senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt). There is a large number of civil servants who will not participate in the benefits of the Act, and it is that class to *which the government should give their immediate attention, particularly when they know as a matter of fact that for the past three years perhaps those least entitled were given their statutory increases, while others were deprived of them. I think if the government do not go the whole way and grant a bonus to each and all the members of the civil service they should certainly give a bonus to those who were illegally deprived of their statutory increases equivalent to the time during which they were deprived of those increases. It is due to these faithful civil servants that their work should be recognized. It is unjust that while one portion of the service got their statutory increases, others who were equally entitled to an increase were deprived of it, in my opinion, contrary to the law, and also in the opinion of the government, evidently, because since that time, they have been giving statutory increases to all the civil servants. The government should consider the representations made by both members for the city of Ottawa, and give these civil servants some compensation for the loss of their statutory increases. There is not a member in this House who wants to see the civil servants underpaid. These gentlemen who entered the service on the understanding that they would get their yearly statutory increase should have faith kept with them, and I trust that even at this late date the government will see that justice is done.
Were these gentlemen, to whom the hon. member (Mr. Emmerson) has referred, granted any living allowance when they were brought to Ottawa ?

I am unable to answer, as these are officers of the Department of Customs. I think it is a provision of the law that when an officer is moved from one place to another without being promoted, his expenses are paid. My hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) was evidently not in the House during the discussion to-day, or he would know the nature of the Bill, and it would not be necessary for me to add any observations now. I hardly Mr. EMMERSON.
feel justified in taking up the time of the committee in explaining to him, as I have explained on several occasions to-day, that this measure does not purport to deal with every class of the civil service. That is a task that could not in all probability be dealt with at any one session. It has to be disposed of by instalments. We commenced to improve the position of the civil servants some years ago, and we are improving it by degrees. One of the hon. gentlemen from Ottawa suggested $50 per head bonus, and another $100, and others improved it to $200 and $300. I hardly think that is a dignified way of dealing with the subject. These gentlemen may be very serious, but they know that their propositions are not practical, and are not such as any government could adopt. It has to be borne in mind that there are two sides to a question of that kind. There Is the taxpayer
It was the Postmaster General who said $300.

One gentleman proposed $50, and another $100. and it was a sort of competition between them, and they were not expressing opinions having regard to the merits. I may be unjust to these gentlemen, but I think we have got to that stage when it is either a question of getting this measure through, or having it hung up. If there are other propositions to be dealt with, and if the government is obliged to consider every case, and prepare other resolutions, and get the sanction of the Governor General to other propositions, I think you imperil the measure itself . I have said so from the beginning, and I say so now in all seriousness, and if hon. gentlemen are not satisfied, it is very simple matter not to press it. The government has entered on this task with an honest desire to try and put the Bill through, and if neither side is satisfied, it is a very simple transaction to drop it. It is not possible for us to enlarge the scope of the Bill this session. That is beyond question. It must either go through in this form or it cannot go through at all. The session is too far advanced for us to reconsider it, and take up new propositions, and submit them again to His Excellency. I am sure my hon. friends will agree with me in that. It is not that we are not sympathetic ; our record shows that we are sympathetic, but there is a limit to what can be done tin u session, and I trust we are now drawing to the close of this long session.

I understood from the Postmaster General, that the increase in the salaries of those civil servants is proposed owing to the increased cost of living. I would like to ask the Postmaster General, whether he can give us any information as to the percentages of increase that this Bill will afford to the various members of the civil service affected by it, so that we may be able to form some fair comparison be-

tween the proposed increases in the Bill, and the increased cost of living. The Postmaster General ought to be able to tell us whether this Bill gives an increase of 5 or 10 or 15 per cent.

I have not gone into the question of percentages. In the case of messengers, porters, packers and sorters, and temporary writers and temporary clerks, they had a maximum of $500 when we entered office, and under this Bilt the maximum is $700, which would be an increase of about 40 per cent. When you get to the higher classes the percentage is less. It is to be observed, however, that when an officer is promoted from one class to another, 'he gets an increase by promotion. For example, the maximum of a junior second will be $1,100 under this measure, and if he should be promoted to the second class he will at once receive an increase of $100 and "'.may go up to $1,500. He will therefore obtain an increase of $400 per annum over his original $1,100, which is about 30 per cent. If he is successful in being promoted to a higher class, the same consequence follows. The percentage in a class is not the real test of the advantage, because that is not his final landing place in the service. He may always look forward to promotion.

I regret that the bon. Postmaster General does not regard the suggestion I made as serious. I made it with a feeling that is amply justified, and I think the country will receive it favourably. I was certainly serious in making the suggestion, and I would again ask the hon. minister and his colleagues to earnestly consider it. I hope the other members of the cabinet will be more impressed with it than the hon. Postmaster General is.

My remark would apply to the whole committee. When various members suggested increases, I thought every member in the committee considered that neither of our hon. friends from Ottawa, nor any of us, were serious in making these suggestions. However, I did an unparliamentary Act in challenging the sincerity of any one, and I therefore make my humble apologies to my hon. friend and to the other members of this committee.

I want to say a word of explanation. Knowing that the clerks in the branch of the service to which I referred had been brought here from the different provinces, not of their own motion, but had been selected and compelled to come here from sections of the country where living is cheaper than it is in Ottawa. I thought they certainly should not be overlooked. The fact that I had not followed the full discussion of this Bill led me to ask for information in the hope that these officials had been provided for.

The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) asked what the percentage of increase under the Bill would be. I have some figures which were compiled on the basis of the amendment which I submitted two or three weeks ago, taking the numbers of the different clerks to be as follows : 90 chief clerks, 150 first class, 200 second class, and 300 third class. Am increase of $200 to each would make an aggregate of $148,000, which is equivalent to fifteen per cent on the gross amount of the salaries as voted by parliament in 1902 The amount voted for civil government was $1,335,159, of which the contingencies amounted to $350,112, leaving for salaries $985,047 Only one-half the increase I suggested being given, makes the percentage of increase 7} per cent for the whole service, some of course getting more and others getting less.
Resolutions reported, read the first and second time and agreed to.
The POSTMASTER GENERAL moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 257) to amend the Civil Service Act.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
Resolved, that it is expedient to enact as follows :-
1.	Advances may be made from time to time, out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, to >the Minister of Railways and Canals, to enable him to obtain, produce, manufacture, use and dispose of all necessary materials, equipment and stores required or used in connection with the construction, renewal, maintenance and operation of the Canadian government railways, and for the establishment and conduct of railway stores.
2.	Stores accounts shall be established, as of the date 30th June, 1903, in connection with the Intercolonial Railway and the Prince Edward Island Railway. These accounts shall respectively be debited with the balance of stores then held on account of each railway, with the cost of materials, equipment and stores purchased, and of work performed, and expenses incurred in connection therewith, together with the cost of establishing, .maintaining and conducting the railway stores, and shall be credited with the values of materials, equipment and stores as issued and charged to proper appropriations or otherwise disposed of.
3.	The balances to the debit of the respective stores accounts so established, shall not at any time exceed, for the Intercolonial Railway the sum of one million five hundred thousand dollars. and for the Prince Edward Island Railway the sum of one hundred thousand dollars.-The Minister of Finance.

This resolution is designed to give legal authority for a system which has existed in connection with the Intercolonial

Railway for many years. It provides that advances may be made from time to time to the Minister of Railways and Canals to enable him to establish a stores account in connection with the Intercolonial Railway not exceeding at any one time $1,500,000, and a similar account in connection with the Prince Edward Island Railway not exceeding at any one time $100,000. This system, as I have said, has been in operation for very many years, but it never appears to have rested upon any statute. .Tust when it began I have not carefully investigated; but it appears to have gone back to the early years of the construction and operation of the Intercolonial Railway. The practice has grown up, and the government and parliament and the Auditor General have assented to it, and up to a comparatively recent date no question has been raised condemning it. However, in connection with some inquiries that were made about the close of last session in reference to railway affairs, attention was drawn to the fact that this practice had not the authority of any statute, and it was thought best, at the suggestion of the Auditor General, to have the matter put into better shape. We have therefore introduced this resolution, no.t to create any new system, but to give legal authority to a system which is necessary to the working of the railway, and which has long been in operation. If the affairs of the railway could all be confined within one year, and the expenses of that year dealt with without reference to the events of any other year, an account of this kind would not be necessary. But, as hon. gentlemen will understand, in the operation of a large railway it is necessary at times to carry over from one year to another large quantities of stores. Under the method which has existed for so long, this stores account is created; and when the goods are purchased they are charged, not to the railway operations of the year, but to the stores account; and from time to time, as parliament votes money for the services of the year, the, goods are taken out of store and are paid for out of the annual appropriation. It is proposed that this system shall continue with proper legal authority. We have an Act of similar character placed on the statute book a couple of years ago in relation to the affairs of the King's Printer. That was for a much smaller sum, but the principle was the same. The King's Printer orders supplies of material, which become a charge against the stores account; and whatever supplies are used by the various departments are paid for by the departments out of the annual appropriations. Another way of expressing it would be that this is a working capital, inasmuch as the department must have money on hand to enable them to buy stores which cannot be paid for out of the year's appropriation. This stores' account is examined into from time to time by the officials and the Auditor General, and
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: stands as one of the assets in the public accounts. I do not think any further explanation is necessary to put this motion before the House.

I do not know that there is any particular objection to the system proposed by the hon. Minister of Finance. What is proposed, I understand, is what is called a credit account system, that is, that a certain amount should be placed at the disposition of the Railway Department; but having regard to what we do know about railway stores and railway purchases and the checking of such accounts, it does seem to me that to ask a credit of $1,500,000 for such a purpose is drawing a little too much upon parliamentary credit. The balance of stores on the 30tli of June, 1902, amounted to about a million and a half dollars. The hon. gentleman asks a credit, to enable the Minister of Railways and Canals to carry on his ordinary monthly transactions, of an amount of money equal to the whole amount of stores in his charge at the end of the year. It seems to me that that statement alone is sufficient to show that the amount asked for is inordinate, beyond any possible necessity of the .Railway Department. No doubt in the purchase of ordinary small stores a certain freedom must exist and the minister should have some liberty in carrying on through his officers the ordinary transactions of' his department, but I cannot understand why he should require a credit of $1,500,000. The only object of such credit is to enable the deparment to carry on its transactions from time to time, pending an audit of the accounts. The transactions of the Railway Department in the way of purchases, must be simply enormous, if be necessary to have a credit of $1,500,000 always at the disposal of the minister between audits by the Audit Department. It is a line of credit in the department to enable it to carry on current business. To say that in a department, the whole purchases of which in twelve months are about $2,400,000, and in which the balance of stores at the end of the year is only about $1,500,000-to say that such a department should require a standing credit of $1,500,000 is to my mind preposterous. I would not oppose any reasonable credit but I think this amount is asked for without sufficient consideration. The Minister of Finance is for the moment the Minister Of Railways and Canals as well and has perhaps not been able to give this matter the consideration it deserves, but I think he will see that, in the interest of the country and the government, it is not wise that such an extensive credit should be given any department. I would say in addition to the point I make as to the amount, that I think some cheek should be provided on the expenditure beyond what we have under the present system. The Railway Deparment at Moncton is subject to an audit from week to

week, but the auditor at Moncton is, to all intents and purposes a subordinate officer. He is not a check on the officials there, because, as the minister must know, if he made himself unpleasant to those above him, his life would soon become unbearable and his office be to let. There is no question in my mind about that. The position which the Auditor General of Canada occupies towards the various departments at Ottawa would be a happy one (compared with that of an official of the (department at Moncton in relation to his (fellow-officers there. It seems to me, having regard to what has transpired in the last two or three years, no matter what political party may be in power-that there should be some means of checking the expenses beyond the slight cheek which may be made by the officer at Moncton and beyond the other more formal check made by the Auditor General's Department. I have spoken to the Auditor General myself as to whether he could not give from time to time a more thorough investigation of the expenses with regard to stores than he has been able to do hitherto. He has told me over and over again that all his (officers are fully employed, that he has all he can do, and perhaps a little more, effectively; but, it seems to me that, considering the enormous expenditure, some $5,000,000 of $6,000,000 a year in this one department, it would be money wisely and well spent, if a special officer were appointed, attached to the office of the Auditor General, independent wholly of the government, independent of the railway officials and of all persons connected with the operation of the railways, solely responsible to the Auditor (General, who is responsible to parliament alone. Such an officer might be sent by the Auditor General at any time to look into and audit any transactions at Moncton, on the spot and deal with them as such accounts ought to be dealt with. Better do this now than wait till later and have another case of the stable being locked after the horse is stolen. I suggest that the Minister of Finance should consider whether, having regard to the credit vote he is asking, there ought not to be a special official 'connected with the Auditor General's Department whose duty it would be to go, at jthe Auditor General's request, and make a (special independent audit of any transactions he may think requires investigation. [DOT]It does seem to me the amount asked for [DOT]by the Finance Minister is away in excess of anything reasonable. If the hon. gentle-[DOT]man would ask for an amount that would *carry the department over say two months, .there could be no reasonable objection.
I point out that in a large portion of the transactions a credit account should not be used at all. Take for example the purchase of a large quantity of steel rails under contract. No reason can be suggested why 394
those accounts should be paid out of a credit account. A claim of a contractor for many thousands of dollars for rails delivered under special contract can be dealt with in the ordinary way and paid out by an ordinary cheque from the Finance Department. I quite admit that for the ordinary purchases incident to railway operations it may be convenient to have a credit account in order that the operations may not be held up by the Auditor General's department in the way that has been complained of. We heard at the beginning of this session that if a calf was killed on the railway the government could not pay for the calf without it passing through the Auditor General's Department. I think that was used as a humorous illustration and an exaggeration of what is absolutely possible. However that may be, I have no doubt that there are cases where it is wise and businesslike that the department should be at liberty to pay at once out of a credit account. The matter could afterwards be investigated by the Auditor General's Department as far as necessary and the account settled promptly, as they are by other corporations. That, however, does not at all apply to the larger accounts, as in the case of a contractor delivering bridges at a cost of many thousands of dollars. Many complicated questions will arise in connection with such payments, the certificate of the deputy head of the department at Ottawa is required as to the efficiency of the bridge and various other questions will arise in connection with such a contract, a percentage of the contract may be retained, and so on. It would be very improper and unjustifiable that these accounts should be dealt with on a credit account at the will of the officers at Moncton. These things should be dealt with as they have been dealt with in the past, and if the minister will say that there is to be a limitation in regard to large transactions of that kind, and that he wants the credit only for the small transactions of a railway company, limiting it to supplies for two or three months in order to keep the railway going without hindrance or obstruction, I will have no objection whatever. But I protest that this request for a credit of $1,500,000 is totally unwarranted, and, in view of the criticisms which we ori this side of the House have felt compelled to make on railway expenditure in the past, I think the demand is unjustifiable.

I am not aware of any question whatever between the Railway Department and the Auditor General which could have any bearing on this transaction. It is not within my knowledge that there has been any difficulty. I do not always see eye to eye with the Auditor General, but in this matter I am bound to say that I am acting at his request in bringing this forward, because lie has suggested it as a necessary and proper step.



So whatever may he said about other matters on which that gentleman and I have not always agreed, this certainly is not a case in which there is any difference of opinion. As to the Auditor General sending an officer to Moncton, let me remind the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) that he has that power to-day, and that he can send an officer there every day in the week if he chooses. There is absolutely no limit to Ills power to examine the railway accounts at Moncton. X am afraid my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) had t different impression.
Not at all.

Then it must be that the Auditor General has not the staff. All I can say on that is that the Auditor General has been furnished with all the staff he has ever asked for, for all pur-' poses. There has been no hesitation on the part of the government to furnish the Auditor General with all the staff that he required, and there is not at this moment any application from the Auditor General for any staff that has not been promptly complied with. Therefore if we give the Auditor General all the staff he wants and if he has unlimited power to send officers to Moncton and make an audit, I really do not see what more we can do. As to the amount of credit, I have not personally that knowledge of the affairs of the railway which would enable me to say whether this is too large a sum. I must point out that we propose by this to open a stores account. Now, if we are only to have credit for a small sum-I do not know what sum is in the mind of my hon. friend, and perhaps he would not care to suggest a sum, but he said only enough for a couple of months' supply, which I suppose would be quite a small sum, probably one or two hundred thousand dollars-our first duty would be to sell off all the supplies on hand in order to put ourselves within the limit of my hon. friend's position. At the end of 1902-I have not the figures for the recent fiscal year just closed -my hon. friend will see that the stores on hand at the end amounted to $1,500,000.
That is what I said.
If we are to have a credit of, say, only one-quarter of a million dollars, we must immediately sell off $1,250,000 of 'supplies in order to keep within the account.
Oh, no.
My hon. friend will only give me credit to the amount of a quarter of a million dollars, and I have $1,500,000 stores on hand, and I must sell these in order to keep myself within the limit.

The $1,500,000 that the hon. minister had on hand at the end of the Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
year was fifty per cent of the quantity that was used on the road in twelve months.

At the close of 1902 we had on hand $1,535,377, and in all probability the figures for 1903 will be substantially the same. I shall endeavour before the close of the session to get that information. It seems to me that in starting this stores account we must have a margin large enough to take in the value of tile stores on hand at the beginning of the year. If it is found that the stores can be reduced and the matter comes up during the short time I am at the head of the department, I shall be glad to give due consideration to it, but my hon. friend will see that the amount should be enough to cover the stores on hand.

I think we can take 1902 as a fair example of what will be required for five or six years to come. The amount of stores on hand at the end of the year was $1,535,000 in round numbers. Now that was about two-thirds of the value of the stores used in twelve months. Of course he must keep up the stores. I admit that, but the total amount of stores used in 1902 was $3,132,000 just, as I said, double what he had on hand at the end of the year, showing that he starts his year with six months' supplies on hand.	Now, I
do think, as I said before, that it is too much to ask parliament to give him a credit in cash for six months' supplies. The object is not that the hon. gentleman shall go ahead and purchase six months' supplies at once. He does not purchase them at once, these are all small supplies of the railway, bolts, nuts, and all that sort of thing that a railway requires, and one million and a half includes all the large accounts that have been purchased for one year, by no means the whole of the three millions is used for the payment of ordinary current accounts. That includes all the large contracts that were settled during the year, and surely the Minister of Railways and Canals does not want power to get in hand at Moncton money to pay every large contract. He may have to pay $100,000 to a bridge company on a contract for bridges. He does not want that money there at all, it is not desirable he should have it there. So with buying 20,000 tons of steel rails that are not required by the Minister of Railways at Moncton as a credit account. These accounts will be settled here, no matter what credit he has got. All I ask is that this shall be kept down to a reasonable sum. As to what the hon. gentleman said about the request of the Auditor General, I am willing for my part to say this, that the credit account should be kept up to any amount the Auditor General says is reasonable, I have not the slightest objection to that. Whatever amount the Auditor General says is a reasonable current credit a'.*-

count for the Department of Railways, confining it to tlie matters that must be settled outside the head office, I am willing should be granted. With regard to the other matter, as to a special audit, I can only say that I asked the Auditor General last year why some special effort was not made to have a peculiarly railway audit under himself, and the Auditor General told me he had not a staff that would enable him to do it; and moreover, he said, the person who had to make that audit must be a person with a special knowledge. He would have to be an auditor who knew something of railway accounts, perhaps, drawn from a bank or a merchant's office, but an auditor having special knowledge of the particular subject. I can only say that I do not cart.', as I said before, what party is in power-no better money could be spent than having a thoroughly competent man to investigate railway accounts and to see that they are kept according to the ordinary system of railway companies.

I repeat that the Auditor General has all the staff that he has asked for. Now I am not prepared to go so far as to say that the Auditor General is the proper judge of all these things ; however, since my hon. friend says he would be content to afford whatever credit the Auditor General thinks is necessary, I can -say that this Bill has been prepared with the full knowledge and approval of the Auditor General, and it is at his re quest that I introduce it.
Does the hon. gentleman say it was at the instance of the Audita" General that he asks for a credit of a million and a half ?

I say the Bill was sent up to the Auditor General by one of the officers of the Railway Department, who discussed it with the Audito:: General, and that gentleman has approved it, including the million and a half for the Intercolonial. I have had no recent communication with the Auditor General about it, but I did inform him some time ago that a Bill of this nature would be brought forward, and he was desirous that it should be brought forward.

As the Minister of Finance says he does not profess to have any special knowledge of this subject, being only an acting minister, I repeat that if the Auditor General will look into this question with a view of the temporary requirement/! of the Department of Railways when wanting a credit account, and will eliminate all the repayments that should be made only through the head office or through the deputy minister, I have not the slightest objection so far as I am personally concerned, to his naming the amount of the credit.
394J

Well, 1 am bound to say that I must assume that the Auditor General has looked into this resolution. The drqft resolution was put upon the Order Paper at an early stage, it was found to be incomplete, and it was withdrawn and another was prepared. Although I have not had a personal conference with the Auditor General, I am informed by an officer of the Railway Department that he discussed it with the Auditor General, and this resolution is introduced in conformity with the Auditor General's wishes.

Has the minister any objection to asking the Auditor General to state in writing what he thinks would be a necessary credit for that account to be used in the way I mention, not for the whole year, but a temporary account to be renewed from time to time, to keep it going, eliminating all the requirements for large contract payments ?

Well,. I do not -see any need of doing it. I am bound to take the Auditor General's approval of this resolution. I -do not agree with my hon. friend that the Auditor General's opinion is the only one -to be considered in the matter. But I am glad in this case that I am able to have the Auditor General's opinion to confirm the resolution.
Anyway the hon. gentleman has not got his opinion.
I confess I have not got it directly, but I was informed that he had this resolution before him, had it in his hands, and approved of it.

I think it would be interesting for the acting Minister of Railways to tell the committee whether, in the conduct of this account, any payments ai'e taken into consideration for the purchase of goods which do not actually pass through the store. Now I assume that a large amount of rails, for example, were purchased and they never passed into the store at all, but would be paid in the way the hon. member for Hamilton says, paid directly by the department; they would not pass through the store account nor be taken into consideration either as a debit or a credit. Now if that is the case, the greater part of the payments must of -necessity not pass through the account at all.
I would suppose that nothing would be taken into this account except articles that actually passed through the store, small items such as the hon. member for Hamilton refers to. Then, knowing as we do the entire account for the year, it is difficult to see how at any time the amount in store will actually be as much as a million and a half. I confess, looking at it from my point of view, if there is actually in store

now, or say on the 1st day of July, a million and a half of goods actually stored there, then I hardly see how the account could be carried on with a smaller sum than a million and a half. But it may he, and I surmise it must be, that in conducting this account large payments for material that did not pass through the stores at all, are taken into consideration, and this account is thus swollen.

There must be some misunderstanding. You cannot charge anything to stores account except articles which go into stores account, and these are all subject to the Auditor General's examination and report. My hon. friend says he cannot understand how so large a sum could be there. I have only to state that the report of the Department of Railways gives a summary of the various classes of items. The first report, page (54, shows that the value of stores on hand at the end of the year were as follows : Miscellaneous, $361,733.53 ; fuel, $253,994.20; track materials, $505,557.50 ; iron and steel rails, $414,091.97 ; making a total of $1,535,377.20. These were the actual goods in store at the close of the year 1902.

Are we to understand that $414,091 worth of steel rails have actually been put in the government stores, and were then taken out, or are they purchased and put on the railway track, and never passed into the stores at all ?

No, they are in stores account, whether they are actually put into the shed or not-I think perhaps not, except it might be convenient to do that; but they are not laid on the track. When they are taken from the stores account and laid on the track then they have to be paid for out of the appropriation so that when they are actually laid on the track they could not be taken into the stores account.
The intention of the resolution is not to give the Intercolonial Railway a credit of $3,000,000 ?
No, it does not give any additional power at all.
It only enables you to have a credit with the stores account for so much as is already in the stores.
That is the case.
Does the hon. gentleman say that with $1,500,000 debited to the stores account he could spend nothing ?
I have the figures for 1902 which show that $1,500,000 is the figure and at the present day I have no doubt that it will be substantially the same. This does not authorize us to
