This item deals with the expenses of the offices of the assistant receivers general in the several portions of the Dominion, with the country savings banks and the expenses in connection with the public debt in England. In connection with the offices of the assistant receivers general I may explain that there are several small increases due to the fact that our estimates in the past have been pretty close and we want to give two or three small increases to officials in various offices who are deemed worthy. In reference to country banks' there is a reduction which is due to the fact that we have abolished one of the country savings banks and turned the business over to the department of my hon. friend the Postmaster General, consolidating it with the Post Office Savings Bank. There is an item of increase in the expenses in connection with the issue and redemption on Dominion notes. It is due to an increase in the circulation which is steadily going on. Another increase is due to the increase in the expenditure for printing notes. As I explained at an earlier stage in connection with tihe supplementary estimates of last year, there has been a very considerable increase in the volume of circulation and in compliance with the general wish of the House we have undertaken to provide the public with cleaner notes than those which have been in circulation in former years. That has added something to the expense. Earlier in the year I had to bring forward a supplementary estimate to provide for the expenditure of last year and we are taking a larger vote this year. There is an increase in item of English bill stamps, postage, &c. Last year the estimates proved insufficient owing to the fact that we issued a larger number of treasury bills than usual and the expenditure for English stamps for these is very considerable. Mre put in a larger sum to meet that item of expenditure. Then, there are the

expenses in connection witli printing, advertising, inspecting and other expenses of a miscellaneous character. We have found that our estimates have been rather close for these items in the past. In cpnnection witli the management of the public debt in England we have renewed the arrangement which we had with tihe Bank of Montreal whereby they become our financial agents in England. Our predecessors in office made an arrangement with the Bank of Montreal which covered a period of ten years. We have extended that arrangement for a fur ther period of ten years with this condition that at the end of five years the Minister of Finance shall have the right to revise the rates so that if in the meantime any new conditions should arise under which we might be justified in asking for lower rates we shall have the right of revision. Otherwise the arrangement is exactly on the same plan as heretofore.
What is the rate now ?
Is the government taking any steps to secure the cleanliness of the notes which are put in circulation ?

We have been doing that for the last year or two, and it to some extent accounts for the increase in these appropriations. We do not issue any notes that are not in good condition. Sometimes the banks hold the notes, but whenever they send them in we are very glad to give new ones in exchange.
Office of the High Commissioner in England, $21,960.

It has been stated in the public press that some two or three members of the cabinet are anxious to take the place of our present high commissioner in London, as it is said that Lord Strathcona is about to retire. I trust there is no truth in that rumour. What has the Minister of Finance to say about it ?

I quite understand that my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) realizes that we cannot afford to lose the valuable services of the present ministers.
I sympathize with his feelings in that respect. I may say that Lord Strathcona was in Ottawa a few days ago, and those who met him will agree with me that he was about the liveliest specimen of a high commissioner one would wish to find. I do not think he has any desire to retire from the office, and I may say that the government of Canada has no other desii'e than that he should long be spared to discharge the duties which he so worthily discharges at present.
Hear, hear.

What the Minister of Finance said about Lord Strathcona is endorsed by every member of this House, and by the people of Canada as well. As to not being able to spare any of the present ministers; it was a question of deserting the 'unking ship.
It shows how little reliance you cam place in newspaper reports.

And some of them are going on the bench.
Superintendence of insurance, $9,840.

This sum is met by a tax levied on the insurance companies which covers the whole cost of this branch of the department, so that it really is not a charge on the funds of the country.
I am proposing however to make a special increase in the salaries of two gentlemen in the department. One is Mr. Blackadar, who is the actuary of the department, and I propose to increase his salary from $2,400 to $2,800. Mr. Blackadar is an officer of very high standing in his profession, and I have the means of knowing that he has had very strong inducements to leave the service and go into the employment of some of the large insurance companies. He is a very capable officer, and he is really making a sacrifice in remaining in the service of the government at a salary we propose to pay him. The other officer whose salary it is proposed to increase is Mr. M. D. Grant. He is a younger gentleman and more recently in the service, but he is a most capable officer, and he is worth more than we are giving him. We will be obliged within the near future to further increase the salary of this gentleman.
Will this increase be charged to the insurance companies ?
Yes. The insurance companies would be willing to pay these gentlemen these salaries and 1 think more.

I would point out also, that the officers of the geological

survey are not paid as well as they should be, especially in view of the fact that they could throw up their jobs here and get much better pay outside.

There is no doubt that with regard to our higher officers, as well as some of these technical officers, they could get much better pay in private employment than they are paid in the public service. I think myself we could give these gentlemen a much more liberal allowance without doing any injustice to the public service. I speak from personal knowledge when I say that we are losing from the public service of Canada, valuable men, because we are not able to pay them anything like the sums they can earn in private employment.
Why not able ?

We have not been doing it. We are making some amendments in the Bill which has been introduced by the Postmaster General ; but .even in the face of these higher salaries, [DOT]I am afraid that we shall have some difficulty in keeping some of the higher classes ,of men in the service.

I would like to have some *information in regard to the deposits of the .insurance companies-what our Canadian .companies have to deposit, whether their .deposits are as large as those of foreign companies, and whether British companies are put on the same footing as American companies ?

I shall be very glad to see that a memorandum on these points is brought for the information Of my hon. friend.
Plant for Printing Bureau, $5,600.
i The MINISTER OF FINANCE. This is the annual grant to the Printing Bureau, to cover ordinary wear and tear.'
I understand that a .very large printing press was purchased fiot very long ago. Has that been paid for ?
I think .that there was a large grant last year to cover that special expenditure.

I understand that there *is a very large amount of printing done outside of the Bureau. If that is the case I .would like to know whether the Government .intend to enlarge the Bureau so as to have all the printing done there ; also, whether .they can get it done more cheaply in their own establishment than they can outside ? ,1 think there were complaints for a considerable time that the Bureau was not at all adequate to do the work that has to be done for the government and parliament,
Mr. HUGHES (Victorial.
and I think we ought to have some ex-j planation as to what the government propose to do.

I would be glad to get any information which the hon. gentleman desires. I may say that it is not the present intention of the government to enlarge the Bureau. We have no appropriation for that purpose in the present year. .
Don't you think you ought to ?

That may be a fair question for consideration.
: Mr. HUGHES (Victoria). What about the outside printing ?

I have seen a statement in the press that outside printing is done more cheaply than the printing in the Bureau. Whether it is or. not I do not know.
: Mr. WILSON. Is it a fact that the government get a large amount of printing done loutside ?	.

I have *seen that stated, and I believe it is correct.
Unforeseen expenses, $16,000.
This is .the usual vote.
, Does it not seem rather odd that this vote for unforeseen expenses should be the same from year to .year ?

Yes. My hon. friend has done right in calling attention to that. With the growth of the business of the country it should be larger. I think the time is at hand when we shall have to place in the hands of the government a larger sum for unforeseen expenses. It has stood at this figure for a number of years.
I did not intend to suggest a larger sum. It was simply a matter of curiosity to me that the vote should continue from ,year to year at the same amount.

There are always chances for some small expenditure arising which we do not anticipate, and, considering the extent of the business of Canada, 820,000 is a very small sum. We had to take a supplementary appropriation of 85,000 for the year last past to meet claims arising. We pay gratuities to the families of deceased public officers out of this. We cannot very well estimate how many of our public officials are going to die between the sessions of parliament. That forms a considerable part of this item, and

other circumstances may arise when a rote is required which parliament in session 'would be very glad to grant.
Salaries and contingencies of thie office of the Paris agency, $5,200.
What does that official do and how many representatives have we there ?

I am not sure I can give the hon. gentleman all the information he wants. Just what Mr. Fabre's duties are in Paris may not be very clearly defined. Many Canadians go on business to Paris and he is able to render them very useful services. An officer has recently been appointed to give special attention to immigration.
I see by the accounts that some $3,000 were allowed for the Paris exhibition, but I do not see why a salary of $2,500 and $1,000 for contingencies, making $3,500, should suddenly jump to $6,500.
There was an increase made a year ago. A portion of it was assigned to Mr. Fabre as an increase of salary and a portion allowed for incidental expenses.

There is a very prosperous old country French settlement south-east of Calgary, which has been there some years and is doing remarkably well. I do not know whether Mr. Fabre is responsible for that.
Academy of Arts, $1,600.
Is that for the National Art Gallery ?
No, this is a grant made the Royal Canadian Academy of Arts, which has an annual exhibition.

I understand that there are considerable sums paid out every year by the government for paintings of one description and another for the National Gallery at Ottawa. I am informed that very little attention is paid to Canadian arts in that connection. I tope that our Canadian artists will receive due recognition and not be overlooked in favour of cheap foreign productions.

Quite recently the attention of the Department of Public Works has been drawn to the point raised by my hon. friend. I ihave no doubt my hon. colleague will be only too glad! to see that any real meritorious specimens of Canadian artists will be included in his purchases.
Mi-. BARKER. What society is this ?
It is the society which was presided over for years by Mr. O'Brien.
No part of this is applied to the purchase of paintings ?

No.
Cost of arbitration respecting the accounts between the Dominion of Canada and the provinces of Ontario and Quebec (payments on account of service rendered may be made to members of the civil service notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act), $2,400.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: When will this be completed ?

I think that we are now getting close to the end of this, but when you get a few judges and lawyers engaged in a ease of that kind it drags along slowly. I do not say that as any reproach, because the judges who are sitting in the arbitration have their own courts to attend, and it is inevitable that there should be some delay. However, the business is becoming narrowed down to very small dimensions and I think the day is not far distant when it will be closed up. It is not easy to wind up accounts so many years after the date and there are many delays incident to the proceedings.
There is a feeling that it has been spun out to undue length. It must be eight or nine years since it commenced.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It has been going on ever since I have been in parliament, some twenty years.

The public is becoming somewhat impatient, not with the delay, but with the amount of work that is put on it without making any progress. Within the last year, as far as I know, practically nothing has been accomplished. While it has been no doubt a difficult work there is a feeling that it should have been closed up long ago.
Did the provinces of Ontario and Quebec contribute anything toward the expenditure ?
Yes.
Probably one-half V
Yes.

With reference to what was said by the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy), I think it is even more than eight or nine years. If I remember rightly, one of the first reports came down in 1893, practically ten years ago, and no doubt they had been at work two or three years before that.
I do not see any reference to that matter in this year's public accounts.

There is a paragraph at page 11 of the introduction to the public accounts for the year. The deputy minister made the following statement:	.
With regard to the unsettled accounts with the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, since my last report a decision has been given by the

Judicial Committee of the Privy Council on the subject of the Common School Fund. A case was prepared and submitted to the Exchequer Court dealing with the points of difference in the account between the province of Ontario and the Dominion. Judgment has recently been given thereon. Steps will ibe token to follow the same course with the differences now existing with the province of Quebec. When these are settled, the only item remaining to be adjusted by the arbitrators will be that pertaining to Treaty No. 3. It is to be hoped that efforts will be made to close that up within the next year. The whole of the unsettled accounts between the provinces of Ontario and Quebec and the Dominion arising out of confederation will then have been disposed of.
So that some progress has been made during the last year.

I notice in the statement of the accounts of the Dominion in the ' Canada G.azette ' a reference to a sum of two or three million dollars which it was stated had some reference to disputed accounts between the provinces. Does that apply to this Ontario matter ?
That arises out of these accounts being brought nearer a settlement.

I notice on page M-18 of the Auditor General's Report:
L.	A. Audeitite, registrar, Exchequer Court, advance to cover Canada's share of expenditure, $2,000.
This is a very general expression and very different from what we find in all other accounts, where the persons receiving the money are mentioned and the amounts are stated distinctly. This seems to be a very general payment of $2,000 to be distributed. I think it is very desirable that matters of this kind particularly should be stated by item.

Mr. Audette is the officer who receives the advance on behalf of the Dominion. The governments of Quebec and Ontario pay their shares to their own officers, and it all goes Into a common fund. I presume that the Auditor General receives some details from Mr. Audette, although I cannot for the moment remember in what shape the information comes. This is the manner in which this matter has been dealt with for many years.
To assist in defraying the cost of the publication of documents issued by the Canadian Mining Institute, $800.
This is much less than last year.

I think that last year the grant was made in two separate appropriations. I know the purpose of the grant, but I do not for the moment remember' whether it was intended to reduce it or not. I think it appeared in two estimates, and that in copying it they Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
have taken it from the original estimate. I will have to inquire as I do not know whether it was intended to reduce it or not.
Preparing and printing Dr. Rand's English Micmae dictionary, $748.

This is a little volume which is being prepared from the manuscript of a gentleman who in his lifetime gave a great deal of attention to the Micmacs. He made a study of their language, and left some manuscripts dealing with it. The work is being done by Jeremiah Clarke, a student wTho lias given special attention to that class of subjects. He cames from Prince Edward Island, but is now in Manitoba. The books have recently been issued, although I have not seen them.
Is this to complete the work ?
The work was begun some years ago, and X think it is all finished now.

I know something of this book, which I think is a very useful one, and one that will be appreciated by everyone who reads it; this is money well expended.
Classification of old records of Canada in the office of the Privy Council, $800.

This is an annual grant to the Privy Council, and has been running for a number of years.
Department of the Geological Survey-salaries. $43,920.

There is an increase of $1,350, made up as follows : $50 to each of twenty-three officers, $1,150; chief clerk and, accountant, statutory increase, $50 ; second-class clerk, statutory increase, $50 ; junior second-class clerk, increase to Mr. McKinnon, $50; increase to caretaker, $50. These are all statutory increases.

If the Minister of the Interior were here I would like to draw his attention to the necessity of increasing the salaries of the superior officers of that department In this connection, what about a building for the geological museum ?
I think it is the intention of the Minister of Public Works to proceed with that geological museum during the current year.
Has the question of a site been settled ?

The matter is engaging his attention. But I think he would hardly like to say where it will be. There are reasons why it might not be wise to make known the site he has in his mind.

Engine house, machine shop, car shop, stores, office at Ravi dr e du Loup, $40,000.

It was $50,000 in the original estimate. One-fifth has already been voted. The work for which this item is proposed is estimated to cost $128,000. It is to build a twenty-four stall engine house and an annex, estimated to cost $61,250 ; three boilers plants, $8,900 ; ash pits, $1,000 ; extension to machine shop, $15,000 ; additional land, $11,100 ; drains and water service, $4,000; excavating and grading, $5,000; siding, $16,000; engineering inspection, &c., $5,150. It is estimated that we will spend this year $50,000. There will be a balance of $78,000 to be provided for hereafter.
Was anything spent last year ?
No, there was a delay in obtaining the land.
Has the land been acquired yet ?
Negotiations are now in progress which, it is believed, will secure the land.
Is there a considerable sum required for the purchase of the land ?
It is estimated to cost $11,100. That is the engineer's estimate of the probable cost.
That will buy a very good farm. How much land will be required for the purpose 1

This
land is right in the town of Rivifire du Loup, and cannot be compared with farm land. You could not get a great deal of land in the midst of any one of our incorporated towns for $11,000.
Railway works are not in the middle of towns. I understand this is at the west end of the town, the railway just passes along the edge of
It is within the town limits.
Is the purchase being made by what is called friendly negotiations, or is there a resort to arbitration ?

I think I have a report before me now suggesting that the land may be had at a fair valuation. I do not remember whether it has been approved or not. It is not at present intended to expropriate. We find that in many cases if you get a valuation of land you can do better than by expropriating. Expropriation is always expensive, because, in addition to the expenditure on the land, there are the fees of lawyers and others.
And the government usually lose.
In too many cases, I am sorry to say, they do. If there is a chance of getting a fair valuation put upon the land without going to the Exchequer Court it is wise to do so.

The only question is that it is easier for the government to grant a favour to a friend. I am not insinuating that this is the case in this instance. I quite agree that expropriation is the last resort. It generally costs more and it will be better in some instances to pay what would be considered an exorbitant price.
Would there be any necessity for this now that the transcontinental railway is to be constructed ?

Oh yes, with the increased business on the Intercolonial Railway it would be needed.
Engine house, &c., at Chaudifere junction $40,000. .
Will the hon. gentleman give an explanation of this ?

This is to provide an 18-stall engine house at Cliau-diere Junction, the cost of which is $44,200 ; building for machine shop, boiler room, repairing cars, and for stores, $8,000 ; stationary boiler plant, $5,650 ; water service and heating, $6,000 ; 80,000 gallon water tank, $4,500 ; sidings in new yard. $20,000 ; grad-inng, ballast, &c., $8,000; coal, ash and sand handling plant, $12,150 ; engineering and inspection, $4,465.75, making a total of $112,965.75. There was an expenditure on this work in 1902-3 of $39,465.75, and there will be required $83,500, of which we are asking $50,000 in the main estimates and in the supplementary estimates we will take a sum for the balance.
Is there a new yard being built at that point, or will you move the yard to L6vis ?
There is a yard at Chaudiere Junction but no building. It was proposed to erect an engine house there. Chaudi&re Junction is close to the proposed new bridge.
Will you take the yard away from Levis ?
It will not be taken away, but probably it will not be as much used as formerly.

Has the department considered whether, in view of the probable changes which will be affected by the new transcontinental railway, all the expenditure will be required at Rivifire du Loup and whether a large portion of it should not be transferred to Chaudifire Junction ? Chau-, difire Junction, I presume, will be a very important place when the extension to Mouc-ton is built and the importance of RiviSre du Loup will be diminshed accordingly.

Cliau-difire Junction will become a more important place and we are asking for a sum for providing an engine and yard accommodation there, but we do not think the operations of the new railway will in any way diminish the business of the Intercolonial. We believe that the Intercolonial Railway will do more business after this new road is opened than it has done formerly.

I think the bon, gentleman will see that by making a central point of Ohaudiere Junction it will affect other points, such as Rivi&re du Loup which necessarily will not require the same engine accommodation.
There is quite a long distance between the two.

I understand that, but it is not usual to have locomotive shops every few hundred miles. Both of these estimates were made before the ministry ever thought of the transcontinetal railway. That work, I think it is pretty clear, was never contemplated till the month of April last, and I would suggest to the hon. minister that it may be well to again consider these two items and see whether the money which is being expended at these places should not be concentrated largely in one of them.
I asked the hon. minister a similar question in regard to the RiviSre du Loup item, but I interpreted his smiling remark to me as to mean that he did not think the road was ever going to be built.
I cannot prevent the heresies and fallacies of my hon. friend.

I am quite serious in stating that an expenditure on works that were under consideration two years ago may be money utterly thrown away under the new condition of things. If the hon. gentleman does intend to go to Moncton it may be absolute folly to expend money that he thought of expending two years ago. I would suggest that he should reconsider it.

All I can say is that these items were thought necessary by the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair), and as we are thoroughly satisfied that the new road will not diminish the business of the Intercolonial Railway, I do not see why I should propose to reduce them.
Is this for engine works or only for engine stalls '!
It is for an lS-stall engine house, but there are some small repair shops.

These items were entered upon long before there was any thought Mr. BARKER.
of the extension to Moncton. I would like to know if the Department of Railways and Canals has, since this new project was thought of, reconsidered this question ? Because it must be obvious to every member of the committee that works that were contemplated two years ago in the neighbourhood of Quebec, whether 100 miles or 200 miles on either side of it, may be absolutely useless if proceeded with under the new state of things. I think the hon. Minister of Finance would do well to postpone these items and the question reconsidered. There is $128,000 being spent at one point and $112.000 at the other and those large amounts of money should not be trifled away lightly.

If I believed, as the hon. gentleman does, that this new line would have an injurious effect on the Intercolonial as he thinks it will have, I would take his view of it, but, as we are persuaded that the construction of the new line will not diminish the business of the Intercolonial Railway, I do not see that I can say any more to my hon. friend.
Increased accommodation at St. John, N.B., $84,000.

This is for a work estimated to cost $111,000 of which we are asking $100,000 in the main estimates and the balance will be asked in the supplementaries. It is to construct an eighteen stall engine house and machine shop. The contract has been let to Messrs. Flood and Bates of St. John. The contract price is $71,925. There has been paid in 1902-3, $30,567.56 leaving a balance on account of the contract of $41,355.
You charge three thousand dollars for engineering and inspection. Is not that done by the officers of the department V
A portion of the salary of the chief engineer of construction would be charged to this item. Special engineers have to be employed to supervise the work.
Are the salaries of the engineers apportioned amongst the various works to which they give their time ?
They have stated salaries which are charged in proportion to each work.
Is it not possible that an error might creep in, and more charged to the various items than are actually paid ?
The chief engineer tells me that there is no question whatever as to these sums being properly charged, and that they do not exceed the stated salaries.
If the chief engineer knows that, I am satisfied. The actual I charges are strictly within the salaries ?
Yes.
Last year there was a vote of 890,500 of which $30,500 was a revote, and I presume $60,000 was spent in this work last year.
According to my figures only $30,567 was spent.
It would appear that your expenditure will be $166,000 instead of $111,000.

My hon. friend is right; the total expenditure would lie much larger than $111,000. The $111,000 is the balance required, and it does not include last year's expenditure. We have to add to that the $94,000 expenditure last year, which would make a little over $200,000.
Was the work let by ten der ? Flood & Bates have the contract.
Yes, it was let by tender.
Was their's the lowest tender ?

Yes.
To increase accommodation at Halifax, $83,600.

This is for increased accommodation at Halifax chiefly in the vicinity of Richmond. The railway is very much cramped for room, and, although the matter has been given a great deal of consideration, it has been impossible to come to any decision hitherto as to wliai should be done. The available land is very limited, and room will have to be provided by buying land outside of the city. We do not care to indicate at present where that land is to be.
You have not bought it yet ?
No.
What became of the $143,000 voted last year ?
This Item will have to stand.

I would like to make a suggestion to the hon. minister in view of the great importance which Halifax harbour is going to assume in the near future. Every one who has been there knows that there is no room in the present city of Halifax to extend the wharf accommodation to any great extent, and I would suggest that the ipinister consider the advisability of securing harbour accommodation farther inland.
Item allowed to stand.
Improvements at North Sydney, $10,400.
What improvements are going on ?

The works at North Sydney to which this vote refers are estimated to cost $33,000, made up as follows : Expenditure at the wharf, including dredging, extension of freight-sheds and tracks, engineering, &c., $13,000 ; expenditure at the station, including loading platform, freight-shed, additional sidings, &c., $20,000. The appropriation we ask in the main estimates is $13,000, and we will have to ask $20,000 in the supplementary estimates.
You spent $40,000 last year.

That Is in addition to previous expenditures. The appropriation for 1902-3 was $40,000 ; the expenditure was $29,293. So that there is $10,000 and odd of the vote remaining unexpended, and that is practically a revote.
That would make an expenditure of $63,000 altogether 1	[DOT]
Yes.
What have you been doing ?

The
work is for the extension of the Intercolonial wharf at North Sydney to 60 feet wide and 200 feet long ; also for necessary freight-sheds and tracks.

these votes will complete it.

The construction of the wharf was. The dredging is being done by the government dredges.

I cannot give that information just now, but will give it later.

May I ask the hon. minister if he will give any heed to the

earnest appeals I have made from time to time for dredging to be done at Lunenburg harbour, La Have river and Malione bay harbour ? When I bear of dredging being done at Sydney, and other parts of the province, and those three necessary works being overlooked, I cannot help thinking that the interests of the country are not looked after as they should be. These are works that should have received attention long ere this. Can I have the word of the Minister of Finance that they will be attended to at an early day ?

Building a spur line of railway from Intercolonial station at Riviere Ouelle to the wharf on the St. Lawrence, $21,600.
What is the object of this ?
This was to build a line down to a point from which the steamer crosses to Murray Bay. It is a new spur line which has been very largely patronized.
What was the necessity ?
Only to afford communication to the public.
How many miles ?
Six and a half miles long. The estimated cost is about $100,000 in round numbers.
That is very expensive for a spur line.
It was let by public contract.
It is only forty feet above the sea. I do not think it was necessary to run a road that far. Are there any other harbours down there to which you are going to run spur lines ?

By schedule rates.

As a result of the extension of the work, this year they turned out four engines, the first for a long time, and they are pronounced the best engines on the Intercolonial.

This is the whole cost of the building. It is difficult for the agent at Eel river to rent a house and for this reason it is thought advisable to furnish a dwelling.

Increased accommodation at Araqui, $4,000.
What is that vote for ?
This is to furnish a new station and dwelling which will cost $3,700, an extension of the freight shed and other accommodation.

In the Quebec and the Matapedia Valley.

It is in Rimouski, in a saw mill district, and a large lumber trade is being done there.

I wish to call attention to the necessity for further accommodation at the town of Sussex. I will guarantee that there is more business done in Sussex in one month than there is at Amqui in two years; that there is more income to the Intercolonial at Sussex than there is at Amqui in that same length of time, and yet we have there an old ramshackle station, built when the road was first constructed, which is really a disgrace to the Intercolonial. It seems to me when so much money is being spent-and I am not finding fault with that; I am strongly in favour of the policy of putting the Intercolonial on the basis of a first-class road; I think that should be done and
is being done-I want to say a word on behalf of this station, the most important between St. John and Moncton. The station itself is a most disgraceful one and the freight house is even worse, while the engine house is a disgrace to any place. I think the hon. minister promised me that they were going to build a new engine house.
Did I go as far as that ?
You did.
I thought I was more cautious.
The hon. minister was in a generous mood and said that this year they were going to build an engine house at Sussex. It is a rough shed put up when the engine house was burned down.
If I said it, it will be built, I remember the hon. gentleman mentioning it and I promised to consider it.
And you promised a new engine house.

Whatever I promised to do, I will do.
Increased accommodation at Ste. Flavie, $76,000.

Among the details of this $95,000 are : Additional land, $1,000 ; new coal shed and trestle, $8,000 ; twelve stall engine house and annex, $50,000 ; new tank and foundation, $4,500 ; building for foreman's offices, $2,500 ; ash pits, $3,000 ; grading and ballasting, $8,000 ; engineering inspection, advertising, &c., $5,000.
Are the old engine sheds giving place to the new ones, or are the new ones in addition ?

The present engines being much larger cannot get into the old engine house. The old engine house may be serviceable for other purposes, we are not taking it down. All work of that kind is done by contract. This sum will complete the work.

Has the minister any estimate for bridging the Strait of Canso ?
No, there is a company chartered for that purpose.	.

How is the new steamer Scotia getting on with her work ?
This is to provide a new engine house and other necessary buildingis connected therewith, also for grading and laying tracks.

I want to inform the minister that during last summer we had a great deal of difficulty with the railway authorities. The town was improving the streets, and found, there a large area owned hy the company, which we call the Esplanade. They have undertaken to sink it beneath the ordinary grade of the town, in consequence of which there is a mud-hole. While the town is elevating the general grade of the streets, we want the Esplanade elevated also, in order to do away with the mud-holes that exist there now. We cannot approach the town on a damp day without getting off the level of the street into a mud-hole. The town at one time thought it belonged to them, and were willing to fix it, but the railway claimed the property and ordered the town authorities away from it. I have been asked by the town authorities to bring this to the notice of the minister and ask that some steps be taken to grade the Esplanade. Is there anything in this for a round-house or for a new station 1
Yes. The scheme of improvements contemplates an expenditure of $233,000 of which we are taking $75,000 for the current year, and provision will have to be made in later sessions for the balance.
Does it include a new station and round-house ?
Not a new station, but a new engine house and other necessary buildings connected therewith.
We want a new station there, it is out of gear with the whole town.
What are the works contemplated there ?

I think with this liberal sum of money we can make Truro blossom.

Now, I want some statement with regard to a depot. The place there now is really discreditable, it is nothing more than an old box. The town is growing and the people want a new station. Improvement at Little Metis station and diverting public road, $3,200.
What is the meaning of that ?

It is proposed to move the station to the river side of the track and build a road to connect with the present road at a point between the railway crossing and the village. The distance between the station and village will be shortened by half a mile and it will be unnecessary to cross the railway.
Why should you make the country pay the cost of diverting this public road ? The municipality usually pays for the diversion of a road.
We occasionally have to pay for the diversion of a public road in order to make the railways safer and to avoid dangerous crossings.
This is not to protect the travelling public along the line of railway ?
The railway is bound to protect the travelling public. We should avoid dangerous crossings of the railway.
What portion of the $4,000 is for the diversion of the road ?
I have not the details.
By this means do you avoid crossing the railway tracks V
It is to avoid crossing the track.
At present the road crosses the railway ?

Yes.
Mr. HUGHES (Victoria. And hy this you will save the cost of a flag-man.
They do not keep flagmen at these crossings. We have a crossing in the centre of our town and we have neither gates nor flag-men.
You have a patent semaphore.
But it does not prevent people from getting on the track.

It gives them notice of approaching trains.
Mr. FOWLER, if we wanted a road diverted we would have to divert it ourselves, and not do it at the expense of the country. I think the same rule should apply ail along the Intercolonial Railway. I would like to know how much is for the diversion of this public road ?
As the whole vote is only $4,000, it could not be a large sum for the diversion of the road.

It should not cost a great deal to divert a road.
ment railway in Prince Edward Island. There the people had to build their own public roads, and the government did not assist them. I remember that a few years ago when a road was required to be opened in connection with a railway station, the government would not give us one cent for the opening of the road. We had to do it ourselves. We find in this case that they are paying $4,000 for diverting the public road to assist the people in that locality. All railway crossings are more or less dangerous, but there are two conditions in regard to crossings which make some crossings more dangerous than others. They are the existence of curves and grades. A crossing close to a curve where the train suddenly sweeps out from behind a bank is very dangerous. This is beside one of the heaviest grades on the road.

speechtext: I remember some years ago seeing that an office chair at an old station on the Intercolonial Railway was charged to capital account. There ought be some care taken about the proper charging of things to capital or working expenses.

Before the committee rises, I wish to say that I shall have some remarks to make on items No. 91 and No. 92. referring to the forming of a dam in the north channel on the Galops rapids. The minister is aware that I took exception to the building of the dam, because it was part and parcel of that new channel. In discussing the matter with the marine men since, they state that they believe that the building of that dam will overcome the great damage that has been done to the water-way by the deepening of that channel, thus causing the lowering of the water above the island. They think that this wrong which I claim has been done for a great many years, would be really overcome by the building of this dam, I do not intend now to object to the building of

that dam. I believe it will probably raise the water again to its normal level as it was previous to this work being done. For the deepening of the rapids, the minister will remember that there was a contract let at the rate of $425 a day for the dredge and tug. If this dam is built it is expected that it will do away with the strong current. The reason I mention this is that the acting minister and the deputy minister may consider my suggestion. If the government will allow this dam to be built, it will be built this fall, and they will be able to judge whether it will stop the water. Should it stop the swift current, the government will be able to have the dredging done, if they d'ecide to have it done, at a very much smaller cost than they can while the swift current is running. At the same time, X honestly believe that if this dam is built, the government will decide that it will not be necessary to go on with the work of cutting the channel. I believe from the bottom of my heart that it is really a great wrong, and I am suggesting that the government should do what any business man would do. It is so late now that it would be impossible to do much in the way of dredging this fall. Then I suggest that they strike out that item for cutting through the rapids, and If after the darn is built they think it 395
advisable to go on with that work, they can bring in a vote next session for that purpose. There is no real hurry for it, because where this work is going on there is a splendid channel now. Living as I do in the vicinity and knowing the situation well, I believe that if the acting minister and the deputy minister would consider this matter, they would come to the conclusion that my proposition is a fair one. I mention the matter now so that before it comes up for discussion again, the acting minister will have an opportunity for considering it, and he will not feel that I have sprung an unfair proposition upon him.
